speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

A statement has appeared in the press that Canadian wheat, which was formerly subject to a maximum price after the 1st of August, and also subject to prohibition of export to the United States, has now been made subject to a fixed price of $2.40 up to the end of August. There is a difference between a maximum price and a fixed price,, and I should like to know at what point this occurs and, generally speaking, the policy of the Government in the matter. The handling of the crop of the Northwest is a very important matter. The Government has seen fit, for what I suppose to be good and sufficient reasons, to assume ai-measure of control, in fact full control, over the handling of that crop. I wish to say that it is not at all satisfactory to have notice that a certain position-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
-prevails and to-morrow that a different position prevails.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is rather exceeding his rights. He cannot in putting a question proceed to call in question the action of the Government.
I did not wish to call in question the action of the Government.

The object in view has been from the first, and will continue to be, as large a measure of co-operation as possible between Canada and the United States with reference to such matters. It was expected that before the first of August, powers would have been obtained from Congress by the authorities at Washington, enabling them to deal with the' question, but the legislation was delayed. Therefore the Board of Grain Supervisors of Canada in order to regulate matters for the time being and until co-operation could effectively take place between the authorities on both sides, fixed a maximum price on an ascending market, the object of which was, while getting a good price for the Canadian farmer, to prevent an undue inflation of price during the interim, which would have had the effect of advancing prices on a merely speculative basis and driving up the advancing price of wheat the price of flour and consequently

In the same connection
I notice that the Winnipeg price of No. 1 Northern wheat on August 23 is $2.40; and the price of No. 2 Northern $2.38. I notice that on the same date the price of No. 1 in Minneapolis is $2.50 to $2.60; of No. 2 Northern, $2.45 to $2.50; that in Duluth on the same date the price of No. 1 is $2.50 and of No. 2 Northern $2.45. I understood the minister to say some time ago that there was a fixed maximum price in the United States.
No, there has never been a fixed maximum in the United States.
I understood him to say that the price in Minneapolis was lower than the price in Winnipeg at a certain date.
At that particular date, yes.

Are the figures I have
quoted to-day correct?

The figures are as they are given in the newspapers, and I imagine they are correct. But the whole point seems to be that the variation in price between times-a sort of no man's land, as it might be called-is considerable. Sometimes the United States price is lower and sometimes it is higher than at Winnipeg. On the whole, there has been a very heavy drop in the price in the United States, gradually bringing it down to what it is supposed the price will approximate when the final fixing takes place, and from day to day there are variations for various reasons. I want my hon. friend to understand that the fixation of the prices has made a certainty to the Canadian producer that he would not otherwise have, and it has been, I believe, very beneficial to him. If my hon. friend will read a late editorial in the Grain Growers' Guide, I think he will see what the opinion of people directly interested in the matter is, concerning the operation, as it has proceeded since the 1st of August. My hon. friend says that there is a great deal of dissatisfaction. There may be dissatisfaction.
I did not say so.

There is some dissatisfaction among some, but as a general rule, so far as my information goes,- and I think it is pretty well founded- there is very great satisfaction with the course the Grain Board has taken.

I ask the minister to have his department compile a statement of the amount that has been lost to the Canadian producer by the prohibition of the export of wheat, since it was made on the 27th of July.

I do not know that11 would be able to compile shell a statement, but if I were able to, and were able to place on the other side a statement of what has been gained by the fixation of

that price, I think my hon. friend would find that the balance would be very much against his present contention.

maintopic: EMBARGO ON EXPORT OF SULPRUR FROM UNITED STATES.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:,

maintopic: EMBARGO ON EXPORT OF SULPRUR FROM UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I observe in the press that there is an embargo on sulphur being exported from the United States, which means, according to a letter which I received this morning, the closing of several Canadian pulp mills. Is the Minister of Trade and Commerce taking any steps with the Washington authorities to prevent .such a thing happening?

maintopic: EMBARGO ON EXPORT OF SULPRUR FROM UNITED STATES.
speechtext: There is an embargo placed by the United States against the export of sulphur from United States territory. The supply in the southern states, particularly Louisiana, is restricted. It is needed for the operations of the United States. Not very much is being imported from other countries at the present time, under present transport conditions. Therefore, sulphur has been placed under embargo, but, although placed under embargo, and although none can be exported except by license, the United States authorities are open to consider representations as to our necessities, which representations are being carefully and thoroughly made.

STATEMENT BY HON. MR. MEIGHEN. ;
On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Certain
press reports of my remarks yesterday attribute to me the statement that the city of Montreal was against conscription. I need scarcely say to the House that I made no such statement. speakerposition: topic
subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House again in committee on Bill 127, the Military Voters' Bill, 1917.-Hon. Mr. Doherty-Mr. Rainville in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When the committee rose last evening we had gone over everything included in the Bill with the exception of Form B. As it is proposed to submit
an amendment to section 3 of the Bill, that will necessitate an amendment to Form B to correspond with the change.
On form C-Certificate of vote of a civilian:

What is that intended to
cover?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is a provision that if a scrutineer, or other officer connected with the election, should happen to be a civilian, that he is entitled to vote under this Act the same as a soldier, as his duties place him among soldiers, and in that event the fact that he has so voted is being certified to by the officer taking the vote, and this form will appear upon the envelope.
What cases of that kind might arise?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Either of the parties might appoint a civilian as scrutineer, or deputy scrutineer. That man, by reason of his functions, would not be at home to vote, and it was thought fair to extend; to him, as well as to any civilian performing duties under this Act, the privilege of voting as though they were soldiers, because that would be the only opportunity he would have to vote.
Why limit the scrutineers? Should you not put in brackets "or the deputy scrutineer or returning officer?"

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
will look at the form, he will see in parenthesis the words "or as the case may be."
That is intended to embrace any others?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

That is broad enough to cover it.
Form C agreed to.
Are certificates of discharge granted by commanding officers, and is a record of them kept at Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not familiar with the details, but I am under the impression that a commanding officer may grant a discharge under certain circumstances. I think, however, that his action has to be approved by higher authorities. A soldier having occasion to obtain a certificate of honourable discharge for the purposes of this Act would be able to procure it from the department here.
Are certificates of discharge granted to men. who were attested but who subsequently could not pass the medical examination?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are cases where men who passed the examination afterwards broke down as a result of the strain, or for other reasons, and were discharged on medical grounds. A man does not become a soldier, however, until he has passed his first medical examination.

I know a good many
men who offered to enlist but who were turned down for one reason or another. I understand that such men are furnished with badges showing that they have attempted to enlist but have been rejected for some reason. I was wondering whether that class of men would come under the head of "discharged soldier." Personally I would think not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would think not.
They would be ordinary civilians and would exercise the franchise according to the general law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is my understanding.
On section 2-Definitions:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I move:
That section 2 be amended by prefixing to its clauses respectively the letters (a), (b) and (c).

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
I move:
That paragraph (a) of section 2 be amended by striking out the words "for containing ballots" in the second line and substituting therefor the words "made of durable material with one lock and key and a slit or narrow opening in the top and so constructed that ballot papers enclosed in envelopes may be introduced therein but cannot be withdrawn therefrom without unlocking it.
In the proposed amendment we describe the receptacle to be used in precisely the words of section 122 of the Dominions Elections Act, which is a description of the ballot box to be used in the elections in Canada. The only difference, if it be a difference, is that we specify that "ballot box" may include a bag or other receptacle.
In section 11 there is a provision to the effect that the key of this box or bag remains with the general returning officer either in Paris or in London.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The receptacle is locked so that the presiding officer who has it cannot open it during all the time that it 
is in his possession, unless he mutilates it. It may take a slightly larger aperture to put in a ballot that is in an envelope with a certificate on the back of it, but in every other respect this provision conforms absolutely to the requirements of the Dominion Elections Act.

I congratulate the minister upon the sense of reason and justice that has come to him in making the change in this section at the request of members on this side. The same applies to other necessary amendments which have been made to other sections of the Bill.

Is the amendment providing for some other form of receptacle than the box ordinarily used in Canada based merely on apprehension that the ordinary ballot box would not be suitable, or is it founded on some experience that it is not suitable?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Our information is that in the elections that were taken a bag was found more convenient. The member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) pointed out that tin boxes would be more difficult of transportation. Even in this country there is no provision that the receptacle shall be a tin box.
Wooden boxes are largely used in the Maritime Provinces.
Were the ballot boxes *sent over to England when the ballots were forwarded in the spring of 1915?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My impression is that
they were not. Hon. gentlemen will remember that in this country the ballot boxes are not furnished by the Dominion Government; they are gathered in the different localities as is found convenient. I think they are usually got from the municipalities.

Is there any provision
for a penalty for the supplying of a bag not of durable material?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No more than
there is with regard to ballot boxes in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no provision
with regard to that.
As a great deal depends upon the character of the receptacle, some person should be held responsible for the receptacle being according to the terms of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Assistant Clerk of the Crown in Chancery has the supplying of these things, and we put upon him the obligation to supply them of the character prescribed. We do not provide for the imposition of a penalty upon all our officers for not doing all that the law prescribes.

I beg the minister's pardon. I did not know that provision was contained in the Bill. I am aware that, under ordinary circumstances, 'ballot boxes are made wherever they are required. I did not know whether or not bags might be supplied in the same way, and in that case my suggestion would be quite in order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They go from the Assistant Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to the presiding officer, and from' the presiding officer to the deputy presiding officers.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I said that we would
amend the clause so as to include in the term "military elector" persons ordinarily resident in Canada who are on active service in any of the British forces or in any of the forces of our Allies. It will probably be very difficult for us to get at them, but it is thought quite proper that they should be given the right to vote, so that if they find themselves in conditions in which they may exercise it they will have that right. In the first place, there is a little amendment to meet what was pointed out by the hon. member for St. James (Mr. L. A. Lapointe). I beg to move:
That paragraph (c) of section 2 be amended by inserting at the end of the fifth line thereof the words "and placed on."
That is to meet the suggestion that everybody called out under the Military Service Act might have a vote although he never became a soldier. He could not have a vote as a soldier unless he was placed on active service.
Under the terms of the Military Service Act, the moment the proclamation is made, the men are called out, but if a man were not actually placed upon the list, he would not be a military voter.
The term "military elector" includes a minor or an Indian. Does the word "Indian" mean a native of India?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We do not so understand it. In this country the word "Indian" has a perfectly accepted and known meaning. We do not mean an Indian in the sense of a native of India; we mean an Indian as we know him in this country and as we have him amongst our troops.

A Canadian Indian. I have some doubt as to the interpretation and application of that word "Indian." Suppose a Hindu, who was a British subject and who may have been living in British Columbia, applied for a vote and claimed the right to vote under that definition, would he be allowed to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think there is any reason to doubt that, even if we did not have the word "Indian" in the Bill, the Hindu, a British subject and a member of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, would have a vote. We put that word in only to settle a doubt. Personally, I believe, if we struck that word out, an Indian in our forces would have the right to vote. I always so understood the old Act although we did not mention it. In some quarters, there seems to have been a doubt, because in our Dominion Elections Act we exclude Indians.	[DOT]

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I beg further to amend paragraph (c) by adding at the end thereof the following words:
And every person, male or female, being a British subject ordinarily resident in Canada, whether or not a minor or an Indian, is on active service in Europe in any other of the forces or services, military or naval, of His Majesty or of his Allies.
This will cover our man in the British forces, any French reservist, for instance, who was a British subject and went to serve in the French forces, any person ordinarily resident in Canada who is serving in any of the Allied forces.

Is there a provision for the imposition of a penalty upon a member of the Allied forces, tout not a resident of Canada, who offered his vote under pretence of being entitled to it under this provision?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no special provision for such an act upon his part. I think the general .provisions of the Dominion Elections Act about impersonation and so forth would apply. We are making this a part of the Dominion Elections Act, and this operation differs from the general operation in so far as is provided here. We would not be able to enforce such penalties because we have not jurisdiction to convict men of offences committed outside of Canada; but to the extent that our jurisdiction goes, the provisions under Part 3 of the Act with regard to offences would

no doubt apply to the like offences committed under this Act.
Is it a fact that there is neither let nor hindrance to the possibility of such an occurrence as I have suggested? That is hardly, T should think, the intent of this measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is required that a man should make oath to the facts that entitle him to vote, and, of course, if he makes false oath, the man undoubtedly has committed perjury. But what is inevitable and what we cannot prevent is the fact that our criminal laws do not run in France nor in England, so that we have, with regard to those oaths, to rely upon the moral sense of the voter and upon the precaution of the officer taking the vote to see, as far as possible, that he is not being deceived.

The officer taking the vote could not by any possibility be held responsible for the acceptance of the oath of a man who was not entitled to make that oath. While it is true that we have no means of protecting ourselves by proceedings under the Criminal Code, I respectfully suggest that we should not leave ourselves entirely unprotected in such a case, and unless already provided for, I would suggest that provision be made that on proof of any such vote having been given, it can be counted out. We surely should not leave ourselves open to the possibility of a number of votes being illegally cast without our being able to protect ourselves against the result.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On a scrutiny of votes, the vote of a non-elector under this part would be struck out, just as would the vote of a non-elector under any other part. We do not need any special provision about a scrutiny of votes. If there be a scrutiny, and it is ascertained that a vote has been illegally cast, it could be thrown out under proper proceedings.
Under some other provision of this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the provisions
of the Controverted Elections Act, I think. Upon a contestation of an election, if the ground of contestation was that the candidate had been returned because of a large number of votes by people who were disqualified, the vote of a person disqualified under this Act would be treated in precisely the same manner as the vote of any other disqualified person. At the moment I am not prepared to define exactly what the procedure is, but whatever it may be, 
there will be the same protection with regard to this disqualification as with regard to any other.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Welland, that section 2 be amended by striking out the words " whether or not " immediately before the words " ordinarily resident " in line 22 of page 1. This brings up the question which was discussed a day or two ago, whether or not a man should be allowed to vote who has not been a resident of Canada. I think myself that the mere fact that a resident of the United States or the West Indies or India, China or Japan who happens to be a British citizen enlists in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, should not give him the right to vote at any election for a member of this Par liament. Such a man joins the Canadian Expeditionary Force for the purpose of fighting for the Empire. He may never have been in Canada at all. He may know nothing whatever of the political questions which are dividing the Canadian people. He would not expect the right-and I do not think it is desirable to give him the right-to take part in the civil affairs of this country. Upon what theory shall he be permitted to say who shall govern this country, not merely during the war, but for the next five years? I cannot for the life of me see any reason why the right of franchise should not be limited to those who are ordinarily residents of Canada. I entertain that view very strongly. I think no reason can be urged for keeping these words in the section, which give the man who was not ordinarily resident in Canada before his enlistment the right to vote. ,
The section becomes more objectionable when we come to consider section 3, because both these sections must be considered together. If the section passes as it is, the result will be that a man who has never been a resident of Canada, who has perhaps never set foot on Canadian soil, will have the right not merely to vote, but to select any one of the two hundred and thirty constituencies in Canada in which to cast his vote. That is giving him a far greater freedom that you are giving to the Canadian boy who is serving at the front. The Canadian boy at the front can only vote in the constituency where he belongs. His right to vote is limited to one candidate in one constituency-the candidate who is running in the constituency where the soldier formerly resided. But the foreigner-
I use the term in the sense of a non-Can-

adian, a non-resident of Canada-the man who may never have set foot in Canada, who has no interest in the civil government of this country, and may know nothing of the questions which divide the Canadian people, is allowed to select his constituency' in any part of Canada. Let me appeal to the committee to consider for a moment what the result of that will be. I am told that in the Canadian expeditionary forces there are several thousands of British subjects who have never been residents of Canada, and there may be more before the election. In many constituencies in this Dominion where the vote is very close, where either the Liberals or the Conservatives are in a slight majority, these non-residents of Canada, by making certain combinations, could practically turn the election, and in that way defeat and nullify the votes of the Canadian soldiers. Is that right? Is it a proper thing to do? On what principle can such a course be justified? One needs only to state the case, it seems to me, to show the argument against it. I do not want to take up the time of the House in discussing this matter further, but it does seem to me that the Government ought to consent to the striking out of these words. Every member of his House and every man in this country wants to provide by law that the Canadian man or woman who has gone to the front shall have the right to vote. Every one is desirous that the mere fact of a Canadian citizen being overseas shall not deprive him of his civil right, and surely, when we by law provide for that, we have gone as far as the 'Canadian soldier would desire us to go. I cannot conceive for a single moment that the resident of Canada, the Canadian boy who has gone to the front, would be desirous that that civil right-that right of expressing an opinion by his vote as to the government of the country during the next five years-shall also be conferred upon people who have never lived in Canada, who may know nothing about Canada, and who have no real interest in the civil government of this country.

I feel that the section as at present constituted is an outrage on the civil rights of the people of Canada. It is moreover an outrage on the soldier electors, who are fighting the battles of Canada in the trenches. By whom will the designations be made of the constituencies to which these votes shall apply? We are deliberately saying that men who have never lived in Canada, and who have no interest in Canada in any way whatever,
and who very likely never will live in Canada and never have any interest in it, shall have the same right to vote, simply because they are fighting for the British Empire and in the cause of the Allies, as our own sons who have gone from home to fight the battles of their native land. Those men have no residence in Canada; they do not know anything about the political situation here. If they are asked to designate for whom they wish to vote, they can say "I vote for the Government" or "I vote for the Opposition." When they are asked "In what constituency in Canada do you want your vote recorded," they will say "I don't know." And as a matter of fact they do not know anything about the constituencies. Who will designate the constituency in which such a vote shall be recorded? Who is the only man likely to designate the constituency? Is it not as certain as it is that the vote is to be polled that the person who will designate the constituency will be the deputy returning ofii-cer or the poll clerk in charge of the poll? I submit to the House that this is what will be done. Now, assuming it would be done, to what constituency would that vote be assigned? In the Dominion of Canada we have over 100 constituencies in which the majorities range within less than 100 votes. The difference between the two political parties in this House at the last general election was forty-five members. How easy it will be to find fifty constituencies in the Dominion of Canada in which the majority for one candidate or the other would be much less than 100, and probably less than fifty. The deputy returning officer in charge of that poll will know these constituencies as well as we know them. That being so, to what constituency is he likely to assign tho6e votes, assuming him to be a hard-and-fast partisan who would do such a thing? In passing legislation of this kind we must assume the worst that can occur, and taking into consideration, all that could happen, could not the deputy returning officer easily pick out fifty or sixty of those so-called foreign votes or nonresident votes, and assign 50, or 60, or 70, or 80 or 100,.to make it certain, to each of the close constituencies, and carry the election by that vote? I submit to any reasonable man in this House that this could be done, and the danger and temptation of its being done is what we wish to avoid. It is our duty in legislating to give our sons and our relatives who are fighting the battles of the British Empire in the trenches

oi France the protection they demand, and see to it that their votes are not killed by the votes of men who have no earthly interest in Canada, and who very likely will never have any interest in the country. It is a mo-st outrageous thing that this Government should deliberately say that men coming from the United States, or from India, or Australia, or New Zealand, or Japan, or Russia, or any other place on God's green earth, simply because they happen to be British subjects and joined the Canadian forces ito fight the bat-4 p.m. ties of the Empire, should have the right to vote, and thereby possibly kill the votes of our own sons wno are giving their life's blood in the trenches. I am sure the Minister of Justice will admit that what I say can easily be done. The deputy returning officer, knowing the close constituencies, has in the hollow of ais hand 3,000 or 4,000 voters who have no local designation in Canada and who do not know where to assign their votes, and he can assign these votes as he sees fit. It does not make any difference to the men whether their votes are assigned to the county of Welland, or the county of Russell, or the Yukon territory, or British Columbia, or anywhere else. If they believe in this Government they say they want to record a vote for the 'Government, and that is done. If they disbelieve in the Government, they say they want to record a vote against the Government, and they do so. But they do not know where that vote will be assigned, or what constituency will derive the benefit of it. Who is to tell them? No one but the deputy returning officer ih charge of the poll. I think it is the duty of this House to amend the clause by striking out the words "whether or not" so that it would read: "Who being a British subject ordinarily resident in Canada." Residential manhood suffrage is the franchise of Canada, and it is the only franchise, except what we are now giving. We are now granting the franchise to minors and men who would not be entitled to vote were it not for the fact that they are going to the front as brave citizens of Canada and of the Empire to fight our battles. Why extend this franchise to men who have never lived here? It is an outrage on the civil rights of the people of the country, and if the Government insists on this clause going through as it is, I, for one, cannot help but think it is the intention, or the expectation at any rate, that these votes will be used in the very manner in which I say they can be used.

I cannot listen to a
proposition of the nature put forward by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) without raising my protest. I make the statement that a man who is a British subject and who has left this country and gone, say, to the United States, therefore, has not the same material interest in this country as a man who lives here, but who has sufficient manliness in him, sufficient respect and love for this country, to abandon his ordinary vocation in life and come across to this land and say: I am going to enlist, and, if necessary, sacrifice my life on behalf of the country of my birth-I say that, in some respects, that man is even more entitled to a vote than the man who enlists here in our midst. I know men living on the American side, who, when this war was declared, gave up lucrative positions and came back to this country and enlisted, donned the uniform, took the oath of allegiance, and who are now across the seas, fighting the battles of this country around Lens as valiantly and as much in the interests of this country as any Canadian. Will you tell me that the men fighting around Lens who lived in this country when they enlisted will not take that man by the hand and say: Good old boy, you have done your duty, you are one of us, and as much entitled to a vote.
And more, too.

And I say it is in the interest of the people of this country to give them a vote. I know a man of that kind, a married man, who left his wife and family on the other side, who came back here and enlisted and is overseas now. Is there a man who will say he is not as much entitled to the vote as any man in this House? I go further and say that that man, having taken his life in his hands, is more entitled to the franchise in this country than I am, sitting here as a member of Parliament, because he is willing to make the supreme sacrifice which I myself have not made, or have not offered to make, even if I could. I say it is an insult to this House to introduce a resolution of that kind and say that these men are not entitled to vote. Have not members opposite exactly the same opportunity of getting their votes as members on this side? The whole resolution is based upon the assumption that the men who have charge of these ballot boxes are going to commit acts of fraud, that they are going to endeavour to make these men, these British subjects, who have come from other countries to fight

for us cast their ballots in a certain riding, and in a certain way. The whole amendment is based on the imputation that the men who conduct the election over there, who are to have charge of the ballot boxes, the scrutineers, the deputy presiding officer, the presiding officers, will conduct the election on principles of fraud, and not upon principles of honesty, justice and fair play. When a man goes over there and takes his life in his hand he is not thinking of the little picayune, petty, peanut, party politics that some members of ' this House are thinking of here to-day. He has greater things and larger visions in his mind, and petty things of that kind are foreign to his thoughts. *

In the earlier ' stages of the war no doubt quite a number of men from foreign countries who were British subjects came over to enlist and many of them are still with our troops. Another element came into this country at the same time, and while gentlemen opposite are very insistent that the men who came over to fight for Canada and who are fighting for her to-day, whose interests are in many cases as great as those of other electors in Canada, should not be allowed to vote, they do not say anything about the men who came over at the same time from the United States or from foreign countries to take the places in the factories of Canada of the men who went overseas to fight for us, the true Canadians. They have the necessary residence of one year, if they are British subjects. But there is not a word said about their voting, and the fact is that it is upon these men that these gentlemen opposite are relying in the coming election. I hold in my hand an interview given by-*
I call my hon. friend's attention to the fact that one year does not give foreigners
I did not say foreigner, I said a British subject from a foreign country.
He has to be here three years.

I do not think that some hon. gentlemen opposite are as anxious to give the vote to our Canadian soldiers over at the front, because perhaps they are apprehensive of that vote, as they are to give the vote to some of the foreign element in their own constituencies. I can understand the hon. member for fit. John (Mr. Pugsley) moving a resolution of this kind. It is in keeping with his whole course in this House since the debate started, in fact since the conscription Bill was brought in. He has opposed most consistently any assistance to our boys overseas. He has not done his part as a citizen of Canada, apart altogether from his duty as a representative in this House, in trying to get recruits in this country. Let me ask you, Mr. Chairman, which will have the better right to cast his vote in this election, the man who came from the United States, we will say, into Canada, a British subject, who signed up and went overseas and is now risking his life in the defence of this country, or a young man who, in the fall of 1914, when we none of us knew how long this war was going to last, took out his commission as a lieutenant down in the city of St. John, and when the war showed that things were not going to be ended in a short time and the risk was great, took off his uniform, after drawing some pay, and preferred to run a garage in the city of St. John rather than go overseas and fight.

What is his
name?

The name will be found in the Militia Gazette, that little red book

containing the names of persons who took out commissions, and his name is Pugsley. Lieutenant J. A. Pugsley took out his commission as a lieutenant in November, 1914.

I desire to say that the statements made by my hon. friend are absolutely false. I desire to say too, Sir, that it is a cowardly thing to attack a young man behind his back who is not here to speak for himself.
What about General Gwatkin?
Cowardly-

I ask your ruling, Mr. Chairman, on that statement or remark of the hon. member for St. John, and ask that it be withdrawn. He said that a statement which I made was false.
ber for St. John, because I am in a position to prove that bis statement was false, and he cannot prove that my statement was false.

I desire to repeat again, Sir, that the statement was absolutely false, and that it is an absolutely cowardly attack-to attack a young man who is not here to defend himself.
Some bon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Put that in your pipe and smoke it.
I am not smoking just at present. I think the fumes are rising from the hon. gentleman from St. John. He is the one who is smoking, and he is the one who is uncomfortable just at present.
Yes, I repeat it.
I ask that statement be withdrawn, and I ask a ruling from the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman from St. John said that the statement was false. I think, under the rules, he could say that the statement was false. It was the statement that he said was false, and nothing else.
Hear, hear.
Mr. Chairman, may I also ask you in- regard to the'word "coward"? Is that also in order?
I am perfectly comfortable.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: With reference to the words " put that in your pipe and smoke it"-

I beg respectfully to
withdraw that remark.

I may say that I think the hon. gentleman from St. John will do a kind of smoking other than his pipe, if he does not mend his ways. At page 674 of the militita list, at the top of the page I find-
62nd Regiment, St. John, N.B., Lieutenant J. A. Pugsley, 17th November, 1914.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As to the other words complained of, the hon. member for St. John^ used the expression "a cowardly attack." The word "coward" was applied to the attack, and not to the hon. member who was speaking.
I understand, Mr. Chairman, that your ruling is that the words are permissible.
Hear, hear.

Then, Mr. Chairman, I want to tell you, and to tell this House, that the hon, member for St. John, an old member of this House, stood up in his place in this House and made statements that were absolutely false and were cowardly in the extreme.
Hear, hear.

And, Mr. Chairman, I want^ to tell you, still further, that I am in a different position in making that assertion, from the position of the hon. mem-

May I ask the hon. member for St. John whether the J. A. Pugsley referred to there is his son or not?

After the statement of
the hon. gentleman, Sir, I would decline to have any intercourse with him. I desire to repeat, that the hon. gentleman did not merely confine his statement to the fact that that young man had a commission, his statement went further. He made a statement which I declare to be absolutely false. I repeat it and can prove it any time.

I am more than borne out by the attitude of the hon. member for St. John. He puts himself in the position here this afternoon of absolutely disowning his own son. The only statement I made in reference to the hon. gentleman's son was this:	It was in the form
of a question of whether or not a man, a British subject, who had resided for some years in the United States, came over here to Canada, put on the uniform, kept the uniform on, went over and risked his life

in the trenches, was not more entitled to a vote than the man who put it on for a brief space of time, and then took his uniform off, and now runs a garage in St. John, instead of running a machine gun at the front. Why should the hon. gentleman from St. John object to that? It is a simple question. The hon. gentleman is moving an amendment to cut out men who have gone over to risk their lives for Canada. He has said that they should not be allowed to cast a ballot in the election to say who should govern this country for the next five years. I take issue with him, and I say that they should vote, that those men are entitled to every consideration. Let me say further that those men who have gone over there are not the unintelligent men the member for Welland would like us to believe. They have shown that they possess the right spirit, and I venture to say that these men who thought enough of Canada to leave the United States, come here and don the uniform and risk their lives, know what is going on in this country. Exception is taken on one point. These gentlemen opposite ask where will their votes be recorded? I confess if I were one of those men, and if I were aware of what is going on in this House, and aware of the attitude of the hon. member for St. John, or the hon. member for Welland, and had my choice and could say where my ballot could be counted, I would say; " Count it in St. John, and count it against the hon... member for St. John; he has shown he does not want to back us up, and does not want to help the boys in the trenches; let me get a crack at him, as well as at the Huns in Europe; let me get a crack at the Huns in Canada or at some of those playing the Huns game in Canada; those are the men I am after." It would be an act of retributive justice if some of those men had an opportunity to cast their ballots in St. John, in order to leave at home in St. John the member who has disgraced the city of St. John by this attitude in this House.

There are some members of this House that so far forget themselves, and forget those gentlemenly instincts which ought to govern all members of this Parliament, that any man who respects himself would scarcely deem it proper to reply to any observation that these members may make. I should not say some members of this House. I think I should have said " one " member. We have in this House one gentleman who has shown himself, on many and many occasions, unworthy of the respect of any man, either in this House or outside of it. My hon. friend from Frontenac knows-his inner consciousness will tell him'-to whom I refer. That hon. gentleman has stated that I have disgraced my position as a representative of the constituency of St. John. He says I have given no support to our 'boys at the front. I do not know the age of the hon. gentleman who has made that statement. I do not know whether it would have been possible for him to have gone to the front, but I am beyond the years when I could go and fight for my country, and the most those who are beyond the age limit can do is to contribute of_ their means towards .assisting our country in the great struggle in which it is engaged.
I have made no boast, Sir, of what I have done, 'but I am willing that my record as to the assistance which I have given, compared with the means that I have, be placed side by side with that of any other man in this House, or any other man in this country. I say that I have .not boasted, from the public platform, or from my seat in this House, of what I have done; but those in my home city who know me know that, in respect of my relatives who have gone to the front and in respect of men who have been in my employ, I have done my part cheerfully and to the best of my ability.
I can appeal to my conscience to justify the assertion that I have done everything possible for me to do; everything that the most patriotic citizen would have felt bound to do. That is all I have to say in reply to the remarks of my hon. friend.

By making some reference to my remarks, the member for St. John himself answers the question whether they were entitled to any reply from a gentleman who respected himself. We must conclude that he is in the category of those who do not respect themselves; otherwise my remarks must, in his estimation, be worthy of some consideration on his part. I also am above the age limit for military service. I have never been connected with the militia in any shape or form. I have never been a fighting man; I have always been a man of peace; every person who knows me knows that that is true. This is the first time that I have ever made reference to the fact that my only son is to-day flying over the lines in France, risking his life every minute. I stand here as one interested in that boy and in others who are over there. I am confident that those who are to-day risking

their lives on the other side would, if they had opportunity of doing so, say that the right to vote should he given to those who, my hon. friend says, should not have that right. There would toe no dissenting voice; there would be no difference of opinion; every soldier over there, whether in the infantry, artillery, or flying squadrons, would say: give the ballot to every man who has put on the Canadian uniform and come over here to help us fight in this great cause. I am willing to place my record alongside the record of the member for St. John at any time and 'at any place before the people of this country-and I think I can make the suggestion with better grace than my hon. friend can. Moreover, I will place the record of my son against the record of his son; we will make it 'a family record, if my hon. friend is willing, .and we shall see which the country will approve.

I have not taken part in this discussion; any suggestions that I had to make I made privately to the Minister of Justice. But I take this opportunity of pointing out that in all ages naturalization laws have been overridden by the mere fact that a man dons the uniform and fights in the service of a country. That constitutes citizenship, and the rule should .apply in all lands. I am more than delighted that the minister is making it the rule in this case. British subjects coming from overseas and enlisting here and foreign subjects serving with the Canadian forces should have the right to cast their ballots as Canadian citizens, in view of the work that they are doing in this great war. At the beginning of the war it was regarded as out of place to give the soldiers votes. I happened to be in England at the time Sir Bichard McBride was trying to get the British Columbia soldiers the right to vote in the provincial elections. One evening I met him at dinner m company with Mr. Lloyd George, Mr. Bonar Law and others. The conversation turned to voting, and these gentlemen said that they could not see their way clear to give the British Columbia soldiers, the vote.
I asked them what they had to do with giving the British Columbia soldiers the right to vote. I took the ground that they had neither right, title nor interest in the matter; that the Government of Canada should say whether or not Canadian soldiers should have the right to vote. I pointed out further that it was unfair that the men at the front should be deprived of the 
right to vote while the men at home-some who could not go ; many who could-would have that right. According to the old Anglo-Saxon English law, the man who becomes a soldier loses no rights of citizenship. The Canadian citizen who dons a uniform, goes to the front and is deprived of his vote has a charge of ingratitude against the country that it would be hard to refute. However, the matter was looked into on the other side and the principle was adopted that the men who don the uniform lose no rights of citizenship. On the morning following the occasion to which 1 refer, Sir Kichard McBride was notified by the British Government that there was no objection whatever to the votes of the British Columbia soldiers being taken. Accordingly, the men were given a chance to vote, although only a few of them could be reached. I repeat that any man of any nationality who joins the ranks of the Canadian soldiers and fights in this war is entitled to cast a ballot in the coming election. I have run a good many elections and I have rarely challenged a vote. I always take it for granted that a fellow who is sixteen or eighteen years of age knows pretty well how to vote and how to conduct himself without any paternalism on the part of returning officers or politicians of any stripe. I remember one polling subdivision where my opponent had seven different officers-scrutineers, poll clerks and all that sort of thing-and I had not any, not even a constable or a scrutineer. When the count was made it was found that every ballot in the box was in my favour. These ballots included those of the poll clerk, the returning officer, the constable and the scrutineer.
An hon. MEMBEB: How did you do it?

I let them exercise the conscience that the Lord gave them; that is how I did it. The agent of my opponent questioned these gentlemen. He said: Didn't I appoint you to act as scrutineer? Yes, replied the gentleman in question; I acted as scrutineer, but there was nothing to scrutinize. Then he questioned the polling clerk: Did I not ask you to act as poll clerk on the understanding that you would vote for our candidate? Oh, no; I did not have to vote any particular way; I was to act as poll clerk, and I have performed that duty. They thought that because these fellows got $5 or $10 on that occasion they would hand over their consciences and their votes. That is not the way the boys are trained in the district

that I have the honour to represent. I could mention various other instances along the same line.
A good deal has been said about -whether those of foreign nationality should vote. In the year 1914 I asked the British Government, through Lord Kitchener, to enrol a dozen brigades of German Britishers and put them in the firing line. It was my privilege to enrol the first body of Boers in South Africa-men who had been fighting against us up to a short time previously, but, who having found that they were in the wrong, expressed themselves as willing to fight in the right cause.
They were splendid fellows, and I had the privilege of meeting some of them in England the year before last. Had the British authorities enrolled a body of Germans who would fight for liberty as against the tyranny of Germany, this war would have been ended long ago, because the spirit would have spread until we would have had the free-born, freedom-loving people of Germany standing shoulder to shoulder with us in this great cause. The German settlements in Canada have done splendid work in this war. I saw the other day that the little town of Zurich had sent 20 men of German extraction to this war, and that a number of them had fallen. Thirty or forty boys of German descent fell on our side at the battle of St. Julien. The intelligence officer of the First Division, one of the finest soldiers, in the service, is the son of a German officer, and his mother has several brothers in the German service, but no more true, steadfast soldier exists than that lad. These people are not machine politicians, and my idea is to let those boys go to the polls. They have earned the right by becoming British soldiers, and 999 out of every 1,000 of those boys need no scrutineer, no returning officer, no polling clerk to tell them how to vote. They will vote according to the dictates of their consciences; they will vote for whatever candidate they choose, and no man would tell them to change their vote this way or that way. They will exercise their own judgment.

When this Bill was first under discussion, I understood the Minister of Justice to agree with my definition of the object to be attained under it, name-^ ly, to ensure that no Canadian citizen ghould be deprived of his vote by reason of his being a soldier. As I take it, the section, as it is drawn, provides that those who are not Canadian citizens shall be
entitled to vote because they are soldiers. That contention receives a good deal of support. I do not, however, follow the reasoning that is given in support of it. If it be a fact that, because a man dons the Canadian uniform and fights in the Canadian ranks, therefore, he is entitled to have a share in the control of the domestic ..affairs of Canada, I do not see why our /soldiers, who are fighting in France or in Belgium, or who are in England preparing to fight, should not have just the .same right to a share in the control of the domestic affairs of France, Belgium or England. It is a poor rule that will not work .both ways, and if citizens of those countries who happen to be in the Canadian forces are entitled to share in the direction of the domestic affairs of Canada, surely the rule should work the same in the other direction, and our soldiers should have a right to interfere in the domestic affairs of France, Belgium, or England. Nobody will contend that this latter suggestion is feasible, or workable, or even right, and I contend that the suggestion, that any person who chooses to join the Canadian army to fight in a cause that is not more Canada's than it is that of France, or Belgium, or England, should have a right to share in the control of the domestic affairs of Canada, is not sound reasoning.

Is the hon. member aware that a Canadian serving in this war in France under the French Government, wearing the uniform of a French soldier, has a vote in France? I should think he would have a vote, and I believe he has.

I do not know as regards a Canadian serving in the French army, but , my contention is, following the contention of hon. gentlemen who have spoken, that inasmuch as Canadians are in France fighting for France, or are in Belgium fighting for Belgium, or are in England preparing to fight for England, they certainly should have the same right to share in the direction of the domestic affairs of France, Belgium, or England, as all those other men, citizens, we shall say, of the United States are to share in the domestic affairs of Canada, because they are fighting, as my hon. friend says, for Canada.
Are not all these men fighting for human liberty?
Certainly.
They are not fighting for France, England, or Belgium; they are fighting for human liberty.
They are fighting for France, Belgium, or England, just as much as they are fighting for human liberty.
They are fighting as Canadians.

They are fighting for human liberty just as our Canadian soldiers are fighting for human liberty. Our Canadian soldiers are in France fighting for France. No one will argue that they are not doing that. It is for France that they are fighting, although, of course, they are fighting for human liberty. We do not, however, insist that those soldiers of ours should have a share in the control of the domestic affairs of France because they fighting for human liberty in France. Then, why should we say that men who have citizenship in the United States or some other country, either concerned in the war or not concerned in the war, should have the right to a share in the direction and control of our domestic affairs, because they are fighting for human liberty in France, or Belgium, or England? The logic of our hon. friends opposite is absolutely at -fault.
It is not, however, on that point that I would take exception to the Bill as it stands; it is on this point, that when we include in our citizenship and within oui voting rights, those men who have no local habitation in Canada, we thereby place in the hands and in the control of the Government of the day the direction, in large measure, of the votes of those men, naturally, to the very great benefit -and advantage of tho-se in whose hands that direction and control for the time being happens to be, I suggest that that accounts, in large measure, for the unbounded enthusiasm with which the proposal is supported by my -hon. friends opposite, who have that much of a leverage and advantage over their opponents in any election that may take place. It is not because of the first proposition that I object to this measure, but it is because of the second proposition. I do not so much object to those men voting, because, after all, there is a -great deal to be said in favour of the men voting who have identified themselves with our country to the extent of fighting alongside of our soldiers; but when in OTder to give them what is claimed for them as their right, we thereby place in fact in large measure the

direction of this large number of votes in the hands of the Government of the day and its friends for the benefit of themselves and their friends, that is a negation of everything that properly belongs to a free franchise in a free country. It is for that reason I find it necessary to support the amendment of my hon. friend.

I listened carefully to
many of the hon. members on the other side of the House who have spoken upon this subject and I was struck with the great trepidation and fear that they showed as to the enlargement of the class of voters. I wondered whether or not these hon. gentlemen opposite are afraid of the soldiers' vote.
We are afraid of the Government count.
You have control of it by the amendment.

The remark of the hon. gentleman shows that he does not know what he is frightened of. He has no justification whatever for any such remark. To my mind, one of the cardinal principles that should actuate any civilized people is the extension, rather than the restriction, of the franchise. I notice that some hon. gentlemen on the other side remained silent and did not share in the views propounded by my hon. friend from St. John, who voted against compulsory military service, though he says in this House that he has done everything to help the boys at the front. A man's actions best show what inspires him, and how his remarks should be construed.
My hon. friend voted for compulsory service. How much has he done to help our boys at the front?
Unfortunately, his son died, the same as yours.
I do not wish to enter into a discussion of my own personal attitude.
I mean, how much did the hon. member help the boys at the front by his vote in the House for compulsory service?

The hon. gentleman says he knows what he means, but I do not, and I will leave it to the House to judge what he means. I do not wish to put forward here anything that I have done towards assisting the boys at the front, because I do not think it is anything par-

ticular to boast about. All I feel sorry for is that I have not done as much as I think I should have done, although I have done what I reasonably could, in view of the opportunities presented. Some lion, gentlemen opposite, if I may say so without malice, who boast with a good deal of effrontery of what they have done in aid of the boys at the front-and those whom the cap fits can put it on-have blocked and questioned every move that has been made to assist the boys at the front, and engendered suspicion, thereby retarding the efforts of the Government. Some of these gentlemen are frittering away the time of this House in practically obstructive tactics. They say that the Government has mismanaged the war, has ma,de a bungle of it.
They have.

The hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) the other night, in telling how the Government had mismanaged the war, spoke of the horse scandals. When one remembers that no less than 65,000 horses were bought by this Government at a cost of nearly $9,000,000, and shipped overseas in one year, of which 44,000 were for Prance and England, and that the scandal amounted to five horses which were surreptitiously passed off at Val-eartier, the horse scandal is not worth mentioning in this House. The people are net concerned about that, but they are concerned about the fact that the boys at the frent need reinforcements, and need them badly, and are crying for them.
'The Government has 'mismanaged the war, they say. Who is. a better judge of that than the soldier? Why should not the soldier vote upon that question? Who knows more about conditions at the front than the soldier in the Canadian expeditionary force, no matter whence he comes? I should think hon. gentlemen opposite would praise the soldier. This Bill does not go as far as the hon. member for Edmonton alleged. It does not presume to give the vote to a foreigner, just because he is in the Canadian expeditionary force, but it is giving the vote to those British subjects, no matter where they came from, who have joined the 'Canadian forces to fight for Canada and the Empire. Does not the man, no matter where he comes from, who becomes a member of the Canadian expeditionary force, earn his right to citizenship? On what higher plane, I ask the hon. member for Edmonton and the hon. member for St. John oonld citizenship be .put in this great time of stress and
310*
trial, when the very foundations of the Empire are being shaken? Do not we welcome the British subject from the United States or any other place who joins the Canadian forces? In what does patriotism consist? It is all right for the hon. member for St. John to boast of his loyalty. No- one disputes his loyalty. But I do dispute his patriotism, and there is a great distinction 'between loyalty and patriotism.
I rise to a point of order. I did not boast of my loyalty at all. I do not think any man should do that.
Then I withdraw the statement that the hon. gentleman ever claimed to be loyal.
I do not think it is necessary in this House, or anywhere else in this country, to 'boast of your loyalty.

There is a difference between loyalty and patriotism. Loyalty is a sentiment, a feeling of love for one's country. A man may sing " We'll never let the old flag fall " for a thousand years, and be ever so loyal, but he would not he patriotic unless he did something to show his loyalty and to keep the old flag flying. Patriotism is loyalty in action -the doing o.f something. This Government has certainly been patriotic. Day in and day out they have had but a single purpose in all their war measures, the purpose of solidifying and concentrating the energies of this nation upon the great task before us, and when the boys in the trenches were calling, calling, and calling for more help in tones that could not be forgotten, the hon. member for St. John stood up and voted against the only Bill ever presented in this House to give the boys in the trenches the aid they required. It is by that I judge his patriotism, even if he does not claim to be loyal.

I must correct the hon. gentleman. It is too much the habit of hon. gentlemen opposite to try and throw discredit on members on this side of the House. I did not say that I did not claim to be loyal. What I said was that I did not boast of my loyalty.

I think the hon. gentleman has very good ground for not boasting of it.
With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton, there is a great distinction to be drawn in connection with the argument he makes as to soldiers of this country voting to affect the internal

policy of France or Belgium. If a Canadian. soldier was fighting in the army of France or Belgium they should give him the vote, whether this Government gave him a vote or not. We are asking that men of British blood who happen for the time toeing to be living outside of this country, who have been moved by their patriotic spirit to enroll with the Canadian forces, get their kits, go into training, and go to the front and die, who under our law can take advantage of the Patriotic Fund, and the separation allowance, if they are married, who are entitled to hospital and Bed Cross benefits, who get socks and other comforts for the soldiers from the women of Canada-we are asking that they shall be given the vote. Hon. gentlemen opposite would give these soldiers of ours all these comforts,, but for political reasons, being frightened of them, would deny them the vote. Do we realize that a war is on, and that to encourage our soldiers we must give them not only material comforts, but also the abstract right to vote? They have taken their lives in their hands and gone to the front to do or die for us. They have earned their right to citizenship, and surely to God they are entitled to the vote.

I very much hope that my learned and hon.' friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) will withdraw his motion. The men with whom this section deals are British subjects, not foreigners, as my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) says. It is presumed that they are British subjects. As such they have come from the United States and other countries and have joined our forces, particularly in Western Canada. My hon. friend says they should not be permitted to exercise the franchise. They have no right to exercise the franchise in the United States, not being American citizens, and in this war more than in any other conflict of the ages, the destiny of the British Empire is at stake. The only opportunity these men will ever have of casting a vote as to what shall be the future of this Empire is as units in the Canadian forces, and not otherwise or elsewhere. I therefore submit that as British citizens governed and actuated by a patriotic willingness to offer their lives 'for the safety of the Empire and of this section of it-because after all their love was the love of empire, they found Canada a convenient place in which to enlist-Canada now offers the only opportunity that ever will be afforded to them 
to cast their votes for the defence of this Empire and determine whether or not in the midst of this war the conduct of the administration of this country merits the approval or disapproval of the men overseas. These men, British subjects, British citizens, coming here and signing on for three years, giving service to the state in Flanders and in France, offering their lives in the trenches, are asking now at the hands of this Administration an opportunity to cast a vote for the British Empire, for its salvation, 'for its destiny, and for that particular section of it which is called the Dominion of Canada. That is the first reason why they should have a vote.
The second reason is that these men have a deep and abiding interest in that portion of the Empire called Canada, because they have been receiving pay and separation allowances from our exchequer. They have an interest in the administration of the Dominion, because, in the future, their pensions must come' from the Dominion, so that they have a deep and abiding interest in the administration of the financial affairs of Canada. They have been enlisted for one, two or three years, and should have the right to say whether or not the administration of the financial affairs of the country has been such as to merit their approval or their disapproval, because they have been engaged undeT Canadian administration, because they are under the aegis of Canada, because they have been receiving their pay from Canada, they have a deep and vital interest in the right to cjust their votes. I. cannot see how it would be possible to get away from these reasons. Let us examine the question a little further. What are the essential qualifications for voting in Canada? Two things only: residence and citizenship, or, to put it the other way, citizenship and residence. Those British citizens come from other countrieis and enlist here, thereby answering the first qualification. The second is answered by service. I said some days ago, and I wish to repeat it, that service given to the State by willing offer of one's life as a sacrifice upon the altar of patriotism, is the highest, ' the noblest, and mcnst enduring service this world can ever know. Who would for a moment contend that service such as that for six, eight, or ten months, does not far transcend one year or three years' residence in Canada?' It is only necessary to be a resident of Alberta for one year, before a man is entitled to the franchise. 1 am sure from what I know of my

hon. friend from Edmonton he will agree with me, thiat any man who has done six months' service in France or in Flanders ha)S done more to establish his citizenship and his right to vote than he could do by living in our cities for any length of time. I submit that is the answer upon the question of- qualification by residence. In the West, as my hon. friend knows, we have a very large number of Austrian and German reservists. Only a few days ago I received a letter from one of the officers who went with one of my home battalions. He said "one of the prisoners we captured was a German officer whom you knew well in Calgary, but whose name I am not allowed to give you at this time." He was a Canadian citizen, and had he not been able to escape from this country he would have voted in Calgary, in this war for Germany and Austria, yet when a British subject comes along from the United States and enlists to fight the battles of the Empire, you wish to deny him the right to nullify a vote such as that. I saw a letter the other day from a young boy, not yet eighteen years of age, to his mother. He had captured two prisoners. He had been wounded, but had delivered his prisoners to the nearest camp. He said '' Mother, imagine my surprise when I found that one of them could talk English and had lived in Lethbridge before the war." So far as I have been able to ascertain, there are very large numbers of those men all through our Western country at the present time A whole settlement of them escaped to the United States, and were able to go across to Austria in some way that we do not know of. It is common for Canadians to capture German soldiers who were Canadian citizens before the war. They were naturalized, and many of those men would have the right to vote at the next election. I ask my hon. friend from St. John if in the light of that knowledge which he possesses, and which any man who reads the papers possesses; if in the light of the knowledge we possess of the recent elections in Saskatchewan and Alberta, and what passed there, he is not now prepared to withdraw his amendment, and afford to those citizens of the Empire the right to vote as Canadians ; afford to them the right to express their opinions upon the conduct of the Administration of the country, and upon those measures that must be taken to give them that assistance and help that will enable them to carry forward this conflict to a glorious and victorious end.
The motion has elicited just the style of speeches I expected it would.

Very good
speeches.

Very good indeed, of the kind, but absolutely far removed from what is really the crucial point in this motion.
I have no desire to prevent a British subject from having a vote, and I never had any such desire. I have no fear of the votes of soldiers at the front who come from the county of Welland, or who come from any other county. The point involved in this motion, so far as I am concerned, is this: What right has any man or any number of men to say they will vote in the county of Welland, or in any other county, without any residence or even a legal status in that county?

This is not to be
a county election; it will be a war election.-

It is a county election, just the same as any other election ever was. It is an election which will decide the fate of the Government or the party, or decide who shall govern this country for the next five years-not for the next year or two years until the war is over.
If it was a war election, to decide what Government should be in power until the conclusion of the war, the contentions of hon. gentlemen opposite might be considered in point. But this is not a war election, it is an ordinary election in the Dominion of Canada to decide who shall govern this country for the next five years. My hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), in his fervid remarks, said that he would be very glad indeed, and that it would be wise, if a lot of these gentlemen who have no legal residence in Canada would record enough of their votes in the county of Welland to defeat me. So far as I am concerned, it makes very little difference to me whether I am defeated or elected. I never was a very ardent politician or a politician who desired particularly to participate in politics for the sake of being in politics. I have represented Welland for twenty-six years. I have been elected by majorities on every occasion running up into the hundreds. If the people choose to defeat me at the election, I am quite satisfied they should do so; they are the ones to choose, but I do not want the voice of the people of Welland to be smothered and killed by the votes of people who have never lived in Welland or in

Canada. Supposing, for instance, carrying out the idea of the hon. member for Fron-tenac, that the people of the county of Welland should choose to elect me as they have in the past by four or five hundred, or three hundred majority.
By acclamation.
Very well, by acclamation. They might do it again you know.
There is no reciprocity this time.

Lightning sometimes
strikes twice in the same place. But, assuming for the moment, and I will take that county for illustration, the people of Welland chose to elect me by three hundred majority, and thirty days after the election, a report came from London: Oh you are defeated. By what vote, I would ask and the answer would be: by the soldiers' vote from Welland in England? But the soldiers' vote from the county of Welland might be strongly in my favour-

How do you
know?

I am mighty certain it
will be. But I would be told: There are five hundred votes recorded against you of men who never lived in Canada, and never will live in Canada. What will the people of Welland think of that?
Why should my hon. friend be afraid of these five hundred votes?

I am not saying I am
afraid of them. I am not afraid of any vote. I am not afraid of my hon. friend or his friends opposite. I am not afraid of anybody or anything, so far as I am concerned.
It is only reciprocity you are afraid of.

I am assuming that these men who have no legal designation in Canada do not know where their votes should be recorded. They will vote, say, for the Government. Assuming for the moment that they all vote for the Government, who shall designate the places where those votes shall be counted? It will not be the voter, because he does not know. It will be the deputy returning officer, and the deputy returning officer will designate those votes in the constituency where they will do the most good. This Government may be entitled to be returned to power; perhaps they will be returned to power. I am not now contending or labouring that quesfMr. German.]
tion. Perhaps this Government could be returned to power by the vote of those men who absolutely have no residence in Canada. I say that, irrespective of all these high falluting suggestions of patriotism, it is not in the best interest of Canada that these outsiders, who do not know where they should vote, should have their votes placed for them by people who are in the employ of the Government. That is the point I take, and the point I make, and I submit that it is a point that should have weight, and that that clause should be amended in accordance with this resolution.

I wish to draw attention
to a point that may interest my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett). Assuming that everything he says is correct with regard to the propriety of outsiders, non-residents, voting, he will have to recognize the difficulty that the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) has mentioned, the difficulty of distributing the vote. Assuming that the Government intended to be fair in the administration of the Act, would it not have accepted the .suggestion made by the hon. member for St. John1 (Mr. Pugsley) the other day whereby the Opposition would have some measure or share in the direction of the affairs of the voting, relating to this distribution of votes? If they had done that, the Government could fairly claim that they did not want to take an unfair advantage of the fact that they have control of the machinery of elections.
Is not the counting to which the hon. gentleman referred in his previous address adequately safeguarded now 'by the recast Bill?

I think the arrangements [DOT]as to the counting are greatly improved and very satisfactory. But in regard to the point raised by the hon. member for Welland that these voters, these' men who are constituted voters by this Bill, who have no knowledge of any constituency in Canada, would have the right when they vote to make the selection of the constituency of which they have no knowledge, all the machinery, all the direction is in the hands of my friend's friends. I say that if the Government desired to preserve the appearance of fairness under these peculiar circumstances- everybody will admit that they are very peculiar-.the party of the Opposition should have some share in the control in connection with the distribution of this vote, that

is, the two parties should have an even break , in regard to it.
Do you not think that is covered by the provision as to scrutineers?
I understood not.
Do you not think it is adequate?

The scrutineers have
nothing to do with the allocation of the vote.
But they prevent the difficulty my hon. friend refers to.
Not at all.
Ii they do their duty, yes.

No, they have no duty in regard to it. The presiding officer is taking the vote. Naturally the non-resident knows nothing of the constituencies in Canada, nothing of the candidates. He will ask advice from the presiding officer-that will be a common thing-as to the different constituencies, and in that way there is an opportunity which ought not to be afforded by this Bill for these presiding officers to .really largely control the allocation o'f the votes of those who have never been residents of Canada. I quite agree with the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. E. B. Bennett) in his suggestion that the Bill, as it is proposed to amend it, will he greatly improved as to those who have once been residents of Canada, because they must specify their last place of residence in the country. But the objection still exists as to those who have never been in Canada, who have never set foot in Canada, who were not born in Canada, and therefore cannot be considered as Canadians. That class of people will still be allowed to vote under this Bill, and, under the provisions of section (e), will be enabled to choose any constituency in Canada which they care to select.
