Giving the fullest force to everything which the hon. member for Calgary has said, and so well said, in regard to the recognition which the country ought to give to every man who joins the Canadian Expeditionary Force and is prepared to risk his life for the Empire, let me ask him if he does not see a very great injustice to the Canadian boy who is at the front, whose choice is limited to the constituency in which he resides- does he not see the great injustice that is being done to him by giving to a stranger, a non-resident of Canada, the right to pick
out a constituency anywhere in Canada in which his vote shall be counted.
If we concede he should have a vote, obviously the complement of that is that he himself must select where his vote will be placed.
Not necessarily.
Surely my hon. friend would not suggest that the returning officer should do the choosing?
No.
He would not suggest that his scrutineers should determine the constituency?
No.
Nor that our scrutineers should?
No.
Therefore, the man himself should?
Yes.
That is what we have done.
The difficulty is the man will not select it.
I have faith in his intelligence.

He will say: "I do not know anything about the constituencies in Canada." He will say to the officer taking the vote: " Give me your suggestion as to where the vote should be allocated." But the fact that there is an injustice to a soldier who has been a resident of Canada in allowing a non-resident to have a choice of the whole 230 odd constituencies is a reason why the non-resident should not be given a vote, or that 'his vote should be allotted to the constituency in which he enlisted. That would limit it. It might be an injustice, perhaps, to have a number of these votes given in the constituency in which the men happened to enlist, but it is very imuch better to incur that inconvenience, and that very slight injustice, than to allow an injustice to be done in .a large number of constituencies. But it all comes back to this, that no man should be allowed to vote unless he is able to make an affidavit as to some constituency in which, at some time or another, he has resided. The only effect of that would be to debar altogether those who have not been born in Canada, who have never lived

in Canada, and who can be described absolutely as non-residents of the country.
That is not the hon. member's amendment. The amendment proposes to give them no vote at all.

Yes, for this reason; that we have to take this Bill section by section, and when we are considering this amendment we find ourselves confronted by the provisions of section 3, which we are bound to take into consideration, and which expressly provide that the man who has not had a residence in Canada which he can specify, is allowed to pick out, at his own whim, any one of the 230 constituencies in Canada. My hon. friend from Calgary appealed to me to withdraw the amendment. I would be perfectly willing to withdraw it, if I could have the assurance of the Minister of Justice that section 3 will be so amended as that the voter must specify some constituency in Canada in which he has, at some time in his life, resided. I would make it very, broad, so that it will apply to those who have been once in Canada, and if my hon. friend the Minister of Justice will say that he will propose an amendment to section 3, which will require that the elector shall specify some constituency in Canada in which he has at some one time in his life had a residence, then I shall be perfectly willing to withdraw the amendment. But I am not willing, as one member of this House, to allow the vote of the Canadian people, more especially the votes of our Canadian boys who have gone to the front, to be submerged by the votes of strangers, of non-residents of Canada, who are to have the privilege, under this Bill, of allotting their votes over the whole Dominion of Canada, to pick out any one of the 230 odd constituencies, and place their votes in constituencies which, in many cases, I am bound to believe, these partisan presiding officers, whose appointment this Government is determined to keep in its own hands, will have the selection of, rather than these non-resident soldiers.

I do not think I can be accused of obstructing, if I say a word or two, because1 this is the first time I have spoken in the debate on this Bill. I should like to point out to the Government that I am supporting the amendment proposed by the hon. member for St. John because I consider the Bill, as drawn, does an absolute injustice to the Canadian soldier. A soldier from the constituency of my hon. friend for St. John and Iberville

who happens to be a Conservative in politics, and would like to vote for the Government in a constituency where his vote might do some good, is not allowed to do so under this Bill. He must vote in the constituency of St. John and Iberville, where his vote will certainly be lost. But a man from the United States, who never resided in Canada, can place his vote where it will do most good.
That is what he will do.

I really am in favour of
the principle of allowing every British subject, who is fighting in the Canadian 'army, to vote in this election.
Hear, hear.

I think they should vote, and should be represented in this House, I have a suggestion to offer, but I am not prepared to say that it can possibly be done, as I have not looked up the constitutional aspect of the matter. I should like to suggest an amendment, providing that, notwithstanding anything which may be contained in the Redistribution Act of Canada, a county at large be formed, which would be represented in this House by a member elected by all these soldiers fighting in the Canadian army who had not resided in some particular county in Canada before they enlisted. In that way, they would have representation in this House, and people residing in each constituency in Canada would still have the right to elect their own representatives, with the aid of the votes of their own soldiers. I offer this suggestion to the Government in the very best of good faith. I do not think the non-resident soldiers should be allowed to mass their votes, and thereby destroy the chance of a candidate in any particular district. On the other hand, I think they should vote in the election, and that their votes should be counted. They should have representation in this House. I do not see anything incompatible with the British North America Act in creating an extra constituency. The British North America Act provides that Quebec shall have 65 representatives, and that the representation of the other provinces of Canada shall be in the proportion that their population bears to the population of Quebec. If we had 35,000 strangers, or 35,000 British subjects-I do not want to use- the word strangers-who have not resided in Canada prior to the war, but are fighting in the Canadian army, or if we have twenty or thirty thousand, we have almost the population

of .an additional county. It is so much more added to the population of Canada. They should he entitled to representation, and I think a county at large could very well he designated for them, where they could elect their own representative, who could be sent here to represent them in the next Parliament.	v
Would the hon. gentleman only give them one member, to these 35,000 soldier electors?

I do not know how many of these non-resident soldiers there are. If there is a number equal to the number of electors of two counties, I think they are entitled to two. members, and I would have no objection to allowing them two. I take it for granted that, of the soldiers who never resided in Canada before, there are probably fifteen or twenty thousand at the front, and that the others resided in Canada before they enlisted, and will vote in their respective constituencies. If the number is so great that they are entitled to two seats, I think they should have them.
Amendment (Mr. Pugsley) negatived on division: nays, 51; yeas, 13.

I wish to draw attention to the manner in which the word " minor " is used in this section. The section says:
"Military elector" means and includes every person, male or .female, who, being a British subject, whether or not ordinarily resident in Canada and whether or not a minor or an Indian, has been, while within or without Canada, appointed, enlisted, enrolled or called out for active service as one of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Militia on active service, or the Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve, or has been, while within Canada, appointed, enlisted or enrolled as one of the British Royal Flying Corps, Royal Naval Aviation Service, or Auxiliary Motor Boat Patrol Service, whether as officer, soldier, sailor, dentist, nurse, aviator, mechanician or otherwise.
A minor is any person under the age of 21 years. No minor below the age of 18 years has been enlisted in any of the Canadian Expeditionary Forces. I submit that the word " minor " should not refer to any person under the age of 18. Further, those appointed, enlisted, enrolled, or called out for active service in the Royal Canadian Navy and the Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve are not on active service. If they are appointed or enlisted in either of these forces prior to the election they will be in Canada at the time of the election. There will be no intention of sending them overseas for service.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: While they do not go overseas, most of them are engaged in active service. A great many of them .are engaged in service of a very dangerous character in connection with the patrol service along the Atlantic coast, searching for submarine bases, and work of that kind. The provisions of this Bill do not cover those engaged on fisheries protection vessels; they relate only to those actually engaged in naval service.

It would be .a very easy matter to enroll a large number of naval cadets prior to the election, who, though under 21 years of age, would have a vote by reason of this legislation. That might very well be done without the knowledge of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, or of any member of the Government. I have taken the liberty of preparing an amendment to cover this point. I move that the following words be added to subsection 2:
(a) "Minor" in subsection 2 shall not refer to any person under the age of 18 years and shall only refer to such persons as have been appointed, enlisted, enrolled or called out for active service as one of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, or had been at the time of the passing of this Act so appointed, enlisted, enrolled or called out for active service in one or other of the several forces in said subsection set out.
That would mean that all minors down to the age of 18 who were actually enrolled or called out for service in the Canadian Expeditionary Force would have a vote; that all such persons down to the age of 18 who had been enrolled or appointed in any of the other services at the time of the passing of this Act would have a vote, but that those who enrolled after the passing of this Act and before the election would not have a vote. A large number of minors will no doubt be enrolled in the Canadian Expeditionary Force subsequent to the passing of this Act and prior to the election who should have a vote; no one wishes to deny them that right. But what I point out is that the organization of units of naval cadets or of minors in these other services subsequent to the passing of this Act and prior to the election, giving these minors the right to vote, would have a very serious effect on the election and a very unhealthy effect on the general sentiment of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to the suggestion that we should limit minors to minors of 18 years, ^ery few would be enlisted under the age of 18 in any event. When a boy of 17 had enlisted and is per-

forming active service, why should we discriminate once we have, in our legislation, gone below the age of 21?
Cadets cannot enrol if they are over 16 years of age.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to cadets bona fide enrolled after this Bill is passed, it would be rather unfair to discriminate against them and to say that they should not vote, although their comrades have the right to do so
If that be so-and that seems to me quite clear, there is only one reason that remains why we should do this, and that involves the very grave imputation on all officers charged with enrolment of cadets of this kind, namely, that this Parliament thinks that they will proceed to enrol, as has been said, battalions of minors for the purpose of making votes. I appeal to the committee. Does this committee suspect that? Does this committee think it is necessary to put upon record that that is our view of those officers?

It is not the officers who are enrolling those men; they can be enrolled throughout the country. As I pointed out the other night, in different polling divisions there might be two or three young men whom they could enrol in the navy, so that they could register their votes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If that can be done, it is news to me. I did not know that there were naval officers sittting at every poll to enrol cadets.
I am not saying that at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Those lads can be enrolled and become cadets only if they are enrolled by officers authorized to enrol them, and at the proper place. You do not enrol naval cadets at every street corner.
Certainly not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is one reason for this amendment that is advanced, namely, that' the officers of our naval forces-and those officers are few in number-are open to the suspicion that they will enrol battalions of minors-that is the expression of the hon. member-for the purpose of making votes. I ask this committee: In all fairness, are they prepared publicly to put that imputation upon those officers? Is it credible that those officers would do such a thing? Those officers are known to the public; they have their responsibilities to the Government and to the public, and can it be supposed that men in those positions

of responsibility are going to bring upon theinselves the execration and condemnation of the whole population of Canada by abusing their position in the naval forces to proceed to the manufacture of minor votes? I must say, with all respect: This is an amendment for which there is no substantial reason advanced, and I would ask the committee to reject it.
Amendment lost on division.
*Section agreed to.
On section 3-Voting by military electors:

I call the minister's attention to these words in line 3 of subsection 2:
Of the year immediately preceding his appointment.
Does that mean the calendar year preceding his appointment, or does it mean within the period of twelve months preceding his appointment? If it read " within one year immediately preceding his appointment," it would be a little clearer. It might be read to mean that it was the calendar year preceding the year in which the enrolment took place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The suggestion is that
the wording might imply that it is not the year which immediately precedes, but the year that precedes that year. That was not intended. I would call the attention of the hon. membeT to the wording. It is to be " at least four months of the year immediately preceding his appointment." I think that makes it quite clear that the four months to which we refer are four months of the year that immediately precedes, his appointment, and I think, therefore, the year referred to is clearly the year immediately preceding his appointment. I have no objection to modify the clause if there is the slightest doubt about it.

I would suggest, to
make the matter absolutely clear, that the clause read:
During at least four months of the twelve months immediately preceding his appointment.
The word " year " might he construed as a calendar year, or as the preceding twelve months.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If no other good comes of this Bill the training I shall have had in accuracy in expression will be invaluable to me. I am not criticising; I am expressing my gratitude. I beg to move:

That subsection 2 be amended by inserting in the blank space in -the second line the word "four," and by striking out in the third line the word "year" after the words "of the" and substituting therefor the words "twelve months."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speechtext:
I beg further to move:
That section 3 be amended by inserting therein as subsection 3 the following:
"If he cannot state or so specify an electoral district or place wherein he has so resided for the time and within the period mentioned in subsection 2, but can state an electoral dis-t trict or so specify a place within Canada wherein he has at any other time resided, he shall be deemed an elector of the electoral district so stated or made ascertainable and his vote shall be applied thereto.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section agreed to.
On section 5-Ballots and custody:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is a very trifling, but necessary amendment that ought to be made to subsections 5 and 6. It is to substitute in those sections the word "forces" for the word "troops," as used with reference to the commanding officer in Bermuda or elsewhere in North America, because there aTe forces other than military forces and the word "troops" would perhaps hardly properly apply to them. Amendment agreed to.

Amendment agreed to.
On section 8-Conduct of polls:

I have a suggestion to
make which I think it would be advisable, if not almost necessary, for the minister to adopt in view of the amendment which he proposed the other evening. Subsection 2 says:
The Canadian military and naval authorities at every camp or other place where any
poll is held shall afford to the attending deputy presiding officer all necessary facilities, and the officer commanding shall allow every military elector, so far as may be consistent with the proper performance of his duties, time and opportunity to vote.
I would suggest that the minister add, after the word "officer" in line 28, the words "and scrutineers."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The amendment that we passed the other evening read:
and, subject to the same condition, to every military elector who may be appointed a deputy scrutineer time and opportunity to perform his duties as such.
Probably that covers it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If it does not completely cover it, we could say "to afford to the attending deputy presiding officer and scrutineer all facilities."

The amendment which
was carried the other evening read:
and, subject to the same condition, to every military elector who may be appointed a deputy scrutineer, time and opportunity to perform his duties as such.
Suppose that a civilian scrutineer were sent. I do not see anything in the Bill, either in the letter or in the spirit to prevent that, and I think it would be necessary to insert the words I suggested in order to give him. facilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Very well.
I would suggest that the word "official" would include clerks, scrutineers and any other necessary officers.

I have some doubt
whether a scrutineer is an official.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The suggestion is that we should say "officials or scrutineers."
That would be all right.

speechtext: I beg to move that subsection 2 of section 8 be amended by inserting in the third line of the subsection, after the word "officer" the words "officials and scrutineers."

speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speechtext:
I (beg to move that subsection 4 of section 8 be amended by adding thereto t*he following:
Every scrutineer, deputy scrutineer, and military elector so acting shall on being admitted to the poll take before the deputy presiding officer the oath in form U of schedule 1 of this Act.

That is the same oath as is taken toy scrutineers under the general Elections Act.

Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I beg to move that section 11 Ibe amended by inserting at the beginning thereof the following:

everything, except the forms.

There is one other suggestion which I think will meet the views of the committee. speechtext:

I wish to move an

On form (to)-Questions to voters:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It will toe necessary to change form B owing to the amendment made to section 3 in connection with which form it applies. I move to amend form B toy inserting therein as question 8 the following :
If you cannot specify as required by question No. 6, or state as required by question No. 7, then state in what electoral district or place within Canada (giving street and number where possible) you have resided at any other time than is referred to in question No. 6.
Questions 6 and 7 are the questions leading up to the electoral district or particular place where a man last resided for four months of the twelve months immediately preceding his appointment. This is to meet

the case of a man who cannot give that information, but who has at any time resided in Canada. He shall vote in the place where he resided in Canada.
I move further to strike out the present question 8 iand to substitute for it the following as question 9:
It none of your answers to questions Nos.
6, T and 8 specify or state as required thereby to what electoral district do you desire your vote to he applied?
This is to ask for an indication, in the case-which now will be, I think, a very exceptional case-where a man cannot state [DOT]either the district in which he has resided for four months in the last year or a district in which at any time he resided in Canada.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.
In the first and second questions a certain form is adopted, and an opposite form is adopted in the third and . fourth questions. Is there any particular reason for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, except that questions 1 and 2 are what you might call formal questions, and it is shorter to put
them in that way-"your name is?	
rather than "What is your name?" There was no intention in doing it, and I cannot see that it makes any difference.
Would there be any objection to casting each of these paragraphs into the form of a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman suggests that we make it read, "What is your name?"
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no objection.
I think it is better to put them all in that form.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then it will read, "What is your name?" "What is your rank?" and "What is your number?"

Does the section to which this form relates provide that the certificate is to be filled in by the elector, or the deputy presiding officer? It is signed by the deputy presiding officer, but it is to be filled in by the person to whom the interrogations are addressed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The intention is that the presiding officer shall put these questions and fill in the answers. He asks the questions, puts in the answers, and certifies that the man has sworn to the answers.
There would be less likelihood of suggestion to the voter if he were to fill in the answers himself, particularly to No. 8.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is just a question of who will do the writing.

I appreciate that the
question of time enters into it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This very matter of not requiring the soldier to do the writing or signing was pointed out to us as one of the things that was desirable, by gentlemen who have had to do with the elections that have been held. It was pointed out that whatever shortened the procedure was of veTy great importance. I am not in a position to say why, but I think it is quite re-sonable that it should be so.
Amendment adopted, and section as amended adopted.
On form A-Ballot:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Queen's (Mr. A. A. McLean) calls my attention to the fact that in the enumeration of electoral districts in which two candidates can be elected, we omitted the district of Queen's county, Prince Edward Island. I move to further amend Form A, as already amended, by adding to the enumerated constituencies in which two candidates can be elected, the electoral district of Queen's county. Prince Edward Island.
Is it understood that the first blank space on the ballot is to be larger than appears on this form?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, the space will be enlarged.

It should be much wider than1 appears in the form. There is no great distinction between writing the name after the printed matter, and marking an " X." There is quite a space there. It might be possible that neither the Prime Minister nor the leader of the Opposition would be able to designate some of the candidates under section 12, and perhaps it would be wise to allow the candidate to designate his party. Some complications might arise in regard to this provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Supposing two gentlemen claim to be the Opposition candidate, or two gentlemen claim to be the Government candidate, we shall be in a hopeless situation.
There is no way out of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have thought the matter over a good deal, and I confess I do not see any way, unless we have some authority which is going to determine the question. Where there is only one man running as a Government or Opposition candidate, no difficulty will arise, and it is just to meet the ease where two gentlemen may be running as Opposition candidates, or two gentlemen running as supporters of the Government that this provision is framed. We have to get some authority that will decide between them.

Did the minister give further consideration to my suggestion the other evening that number two should be number one, number three should be number two, and number four should be number three? It should be arranged so that the first option is the Government candidate, the second the Opposition, the third the Independent candidate, and the fourth the individual candidate who might not be covered iby any of the three.
That is a discouragement to the personal vote, which we should encourage.

I think it would be a wise arrangement, because nine-tenths of'the votes will be for the Government or Opposition candidates, and they would naturally like to mark their ballots in the first or second space. If they do not wish to vote for the Government, Opposition, or Independent candidates, they can indicate some other candidate for whom they wish to vote. The present arrangement is going to be puzzling. A voter may desire to vote for a certain candidate, and will write his name in the first space. If that candidate happens to be the Government candidate the voter will put a cross against number two, and thus the ballot will be marked in two places.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In that case, if the candidate he names is the Government candidate, the voter has twice indicated his intention. We have provided that if a man inserts a name and then makes a mark, say, against "Government candidate" and it turns out that the man whose name he put down is really the candidate of the Opposition, the vote will be counted for the Opposition candidate. The purpose of asking the voter to vote either for the Government or for the Opposition is that the name of the individual candidate for whom he voted may be ascertained. Wherever the individual does know the candi-
date's name, you are saved the additional operation, with possible errors, of transmitting to a particular candidate a vote that is marked for the Government or for the Opposition. After all, the election in each constituency is between particular candidates, and the thing to be found out is the name of the individual candidate for whom the voter voted.
I think the question whether more men will vote for a particular candidate than for Government or Opposition, or vice versa, is in the realm of speculation. The hon. gentleman anticipates that more ballots will be marked for Government or for Opposition than for individual names. We have taken pains to provide machinery by which the names of candidates in all constituencies may be brought to the knowledge of the military electors, and I anticipate that the greater number of votes will be for particular candidates. I think that the sense of the committee, when the matter was discussed, seemed to be rather in favour of the first space being that in which the name should be written.

I think that the very
reverse of that suggested by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) would happen. The soldier from Canada who knows the constituency from which he comes and the names of the candidates in that constituency will vote for the candidate of his choice. Undoubtedly a section of voters do not know who the candidates are, what the constituencies are, or who they are voting for-except that they are voting for the Government. That class,
I understand, would come within the purview of what the member for St. Antoine has said. The military electors from Canada, however, will vote, I think, more generally for individual candidates than for Government or the Opposition.

In view of the fact that there is no distinguishing mark on the ballot-that the ballot does not contain the returning officer's initials-some provision should be made that the person who prints these ballots in London or in Paris will make an affidavit similar to that made by the printer of ballots in Canada. Under the Dominion Elections Act the printer haa to make .a positive affidavit that he has printed so many ballots and no more. It would be a simple matter for a printer employed in London to1 print ballots and send them out by the thousands, as they are wanted, to any applicant who would pay the price. It is true that the law says that the ballot

shall be marked in the presence of the returning officer, but the provision is that it must be marked in such a (way that the officer will not know how he votes, and it would be a very simple matter to- substitute one ballot for another.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no objection to accepting that suggestion. The best way would be to lift the section of the Dominion Elections Act right in there. I move that the following provision be inserted as subsection 3 of section 5:
The printer shall, upon delivering the ballot papers to the Assistant Clerk of the Crown in1 Chancery, file in his hands an affidavit setting! forth the description of the ballots so printed by him, the number of ballots supplied by him and the fact that no other ballot papers have been supplied by him to any one else.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.
Would it not be wise to state in form A that the cross with which a man marks his ballot shall be marked with a particular kind of pencil or pen?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I hardly think,we ought to do that, im view of possible conditions. There was an amendment which I thought had been passed the other evening, but I find that it has been overlooked. It was an amendment prescribing that when the presiding officer appoints his deputy presiding officer he shall give due notice to the scrutineers of each party.
I now move to amend paragraph (e) of subsection 1 of section 4 by adding thereto the following:
Every presiding officer shall notify in writing, by mail or other expeditious means, the scrutineer of each party whose place of address may be nearest to him of the names of all deputy presiding officers appointed by him.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.
I suppose the minister will have this Bill reprinted before it is read the third time? It is rather confusing, and we would all like to have an opportunity to go over it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Will the minister look at form A again? Would it not be well to change the first and last sections so that the first shall be last, and the last first?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It was agreed that that should be done, but I find that the amendment was not drawn up so as to meet that.
Is there any better word than the word "party" there?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What would be the suggestion with regard to that word?

There is apt to be a confusion as to whether the word "party" means "person" or a particular party .as represented by the Government, Opposition or independent candidate. We spoke of that the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
For the purpose of
clearing that up, we substituted for the words "particular person" the words "particular candidate or candidates designated by name," and when we put in contradistinction to each other a party or a particular candidate or candidates designated by name, I would think, under these circumstances, the word "party" could mean nothing other than a political party. Nobody could then confuse it with person, 'and it is a little difficult to find another word to substitute for ''party" for that purpose that would be any clearer unless we had a long description. I move to amend form A by making the instructions as to the method of voting for a particular candidate or candidates precede that as to the method of voting for a party. When this amendment is carried we shall have Form A printed in that way.
Has the ballot as it appears in the draft Bill been altered? Has there been an addition to provide for voting for a labour candidate?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: An amendment carried to make that addition and also to widen the spaces. Furthermore, we substituted for the word "person" the words "candidate or candidates designated by name." That was to clear up the distinction between a party and a person.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.
Will the Government assume any responsibility in the matter oi informing the voters overseas as to the nomination of candidates? That, of course, is not a matter within the scope of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 6 makes a
special provision imposing the duty upon the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to send the information and upon all officers to circulate it in every possible way.

That is all very well, but unless the information is over there in good
time-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It will be sent by cable on nomination day.
Bill reported, amendments read the first and second time, and concurred in.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Rainville in the Chair.
Supplementary Estimates, 1917-18-Immigration-Salaries of agents and employees in Canada, Great Britain and foreign countries->
Further amount required, $20,000.

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext:
['Ryan was acting as a switchman on December 22 last. It appears that he fell off the car and a train backed over him. He leaves a wife and two children-a boy four years old and a girl nine months old-in very poor circumstances.
Progress reported.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Hazen, the House adjourned at 10.34 p.m.
Saturday, August 25, 1917.']

The House will remember that when my Estimates were up before I was asked if it was the intention to increase the salaries of members of the Outside Service, and I replied that it was my intention to have an item in the Supplementary Estimates to provide for an increase in the Outside Service similar to the increase provided for the Inside Service under the legislation of the Minister of Finance, namely, that in deserving .cases those in receipt of less than $1,000 per annum should receive an increase of $100 a year.	.
The higher salaried agents receive no increase?
No.
In how many countries outside of Canada and Great Britain are agents employed?
Only in the United States, where we have seventeen agents at the present time.
Is the movement of people from the United States increasing?

I think possibly there was in increase of 50 per cent this year over last. Immigration from the United States was down to a minimum in 1915, but there was a considerable increase in 1916, and this year again there has been a large increase until very recently. It is possible, however, that conscription in the United States may have the effect of checking immigration.
Is the increase largely among men looking for homestead lands, or among those desiring to purchase lands?

Both. This year there is possibly a larger influx of those who are purchasing land. Quite a number are also going into the Peace River country and taking up homesteads. Our information is that those who are coming over consist

of agriculturists, agricultural labourers, and those with money of their own who have sold out their properties in the United States with the idea of buying cheaper land in Canada.	_
Would it be correct to say that the Peace River district is attracting a larger number than other sections of Canada?
Yes, as regards homesteads.

Are there any special agents from the province of Quebec working among the French of the United States with a view to getting them back to this country as settlers? If there are any such agents, I should like to know how many there are, how many settlers they brought back to Canada last year, where they were settled, and what money has been spent on these agents for salaries and expenses. There is another point:	It has been
rumoured that agents from the province of Quebec working among their compatriots in the United States, in the New England states presumably, have taken advantage of their position as immigration agents to transport people, not from the United States but from Ontario and Quebec to the Northwest. If anything of that kind has gone on-I do not say it has, but I have heard rumours to that effect-I do not think it is exactly what was intended by appointing immigration agents. The idea in appointing them was not that they should arrange for the transport of -men from one province to another, but to get people from outside to come into this country. I should like to know if this rumour is well founded, and to what extent this thing has been going on in the past, if at all.

Before the minister
answers my hon. friend, I should like to say that this is the first time I have ever heard of any such scheme. If there is any truth, or any semblance of truth, in the rumour that agents appointed to promote immigration from the United States to Canada are sending to the Northwest people from the province of Quebec or other provinces, under the pretext that they are immigrants from the United States, I would urge the Minister of the Interior to order at once a very thorough investigation to ascertain the facts.

From time immemorial agents have been working amongst the French Canadians who migrated from Canada, principally from the province of

Quebec, many years ago, to work in the mills of the New England states.
Their children have been growing up, and it has been the desire to secure our fair share of immigrants from the United States, including the repatriation of Canadians who have gone to the New England States. Colonization agents have been employed for that purpose for many years past under this Government and under preceding governments. I understand there are three of those gentlemen working in the New England States, Rev. J. B. H. Giroux, whose headquarters are at Montreal and whose salary is $600 per annum; Rev. J. B. Bourassa, whose headquarters are at Montreal and whose salary is $1,200 per annum, and Rev. O. Corbeil, whose salary is $600. We have no. separate statistics as to the number of French Canadians brought into Canada from the United States. They are all classed as immigrants. Roughly speaking, however, I should say about fifteen per cent of those coming back to Canada from the New England States are repatriated Canadians. They are not classified-as French Canadians, English Canadians, etc,-they are all repatriated Canadians. The idea is that a propaganda should not be carried on in any one province to get a movement into another province. There were some complaints made to me on that score about two years ago against one particular colonization agent. He was at my office one day, and I told him about these complaints, explaining that the province of Quebec had objected to any propaganda tending to take their people away and locate them in the northern portion of Ontario, or any other province. I told him we were not spending money for that purpose. He said he had not been carrying out any policy of that character except in a few -instances where he knew the people were about to move away from Quebec to the United States, and rather than see them leave Canada entirely, he had done his best to get them to settle in other provinces of the Dominion.

Can the minister give me any idea as to the numbers, or as to what part of the country they have settled in; also the total amount expended through these three agents? I would also ask why there is a difference in the salaries. I notice two of the agents receive $600, and the other $1,200. Is it accounted for by the difference in the time they spend at the work?

I believe Rev. Mr. Bourassa receives the larger salary because he devotes more of his. time to the work. As a matter of fact, he devotes his entire time to it. He is very much more energetic and he has brought in many more immigrants from the New England States than the other two gentlemen have. I think one of these agents is temporarily taking the place of another gentleman who went to the front. It is impossible to give even an approximate idea as to the number of immigrants who have been brought in by these officials. All I can. tell my hon. friend is that about fifteen per cent of the total immigrants from the United States are repatriated Canadians. Some of them are located along the Transcontinental railway, in the northern portions of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, some of them are taken right through to Saskatchewan and Alberta. There is quite a colony in Northern Alberta, and quite a colony at Prince Albert.
What is the cost?
There is no cost to the country,"over and above the salaries, paid to the gentlemen I have named.
Are the expenses of those agents paid?

Their travelling expenses are paid. The expenses do not amount to very much. As a matter of fact, I think they are supplied with passes by the transportation companies. There is no per capita allowance or anything of that kind.

From the explanations given by the minister, it would 6eem to me that the department spends very little in what I consider to be a splendid field for excellent immigration. Of course, it is always good policy to get the best class of immigrants for Canada. I have frequently heard if admitted on the floor of this House that the best immigrants who have settled in the West are those who came from the United States. The best amongst those American immigrants ought to be our own people-the Canadians who have gone across the 'boundary line years ago to settle in the United States when times w-re hard in Canada. A Canadian visiting the New England States is amazed to find so many Canadians. One would find hundreds and Indeed .thousands of Canadians at the Canadian clubs in and around Boston. As a matter of fact they say Boston is only an annex of Nova Scotia. There are thousands



of Canadians, and especially French Canadians, around Lowell, Lawrence, Holyoke, Springfield and other cities in the New England States. I am told there are over 30,000 Canadians in Chicago; and there are large numbers of Canadians in Philadelphia, Buffalo and Cleveland. If the department could bring those Canadians back to Canada, certainly it is the best policy to follow, and the country ought to congratulate the Government on the large number of Canadians who have been induced to return. The latest statistics show that there are nearly one million French Canadians in the United IStates. Some years ago, in company with the then Speaker of the Senate, Hon. Mr. Dandurand, I had the honour to represent the Dominion of Canada at the semi-centennial celebration of the Sault Ste. Marie canal, in the state of
9 p.m. Michigan. We addressed a gathering of perhaps five thousand or six thousand people, and we had to speak in French as well as in English, because of the large number of French Canadians present. All those French Canadians are the sons of farmers, and are excellent farmers themselves when they return to the land. It seems to me it is good policy on the part of the department [DOT]to induce those farmers to return to Canada. If my hon. friend has travelled through the valley of the St. Lawrence in the province of Quebec, he will have noticed that the farms are already occupied, and those long narrow strips are not sufficient to maintain large families, so the sons emigrated, and now when they return to the land it is quite natural they should go to the West, where there are such immense domains for those who have any farming propensities. I am told there are excellent colonies of these French Canadians in the West. Some years ago a gentleman brought from" the United States several hundred French Canadians and founded two colonies, and there are some pf them settled in the Peace river country. I commend that policy to my hon. friend and I hope he will bring back many .more thousands of French Canadians from the United States.
Seed grain to settlers on unpatented lands in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, $100,000.	i
Will the minister be good enough to explain this item?

In the early part of August last year there was a very heavy frost in the Peace River country which destroyed much of the crop, and it was represented to the department this spring

that many homesteaders there could not seed their lands. The department sent in officers who visited the different paints m the Peace River, Grande Prairie and Spirit River country, in co-operation with officers from the Provincial Government of Alberta. The Provincial Government supplied se,ed to those needy farmers who had their lands patented and the Dominion Government supplied it to homesteaders. Sufficient good seed was 'found among some of the farmers in that country to supply all needs, so that we avoided the expense of shipping grain in.
What amount was supplied by the Provincial Government in the Peace River country?
We have no record of that.
And what amount of this money?
We have not it differentiated as to the particular portions of the country. The bulk of it was supplied to the Peace River farmers.
Reverting to the item of salaries, how many persons connected with the Immigration Department in North Sydney will participate in the proposed increase, and who are they?
We have an agent named Dooley at North Sydney who receives $1,100, so that he will not receive the $100 given to those receiving less than $1,000. There is a medical inspector who receives $1,000.
Has there been some difficulty recently with regard to Newfoundlanders wishing to return to their country though the port of North Sydney?

There was some difficulty because of the Order in Council passed to prevent men of military age leaving Canada. An appeal was made in the case of Newfoundlanders, and I gave instructions to allow them to go to their own homes.
Was the seed supplied in Northern Alberta largely barley, or was it wheat, oats and barley, and what prices were paid?

Wheat, oats, barley and flax. We supplied 21,712 bushels of wheat, at an average cost of $1.76 per bushel; of oats, 42,486 bushels, at an average cost of 67 cents; of barley, 1,696 bushels, at an average cost of $1.03 per bushel; and of flax, 533 bushels, at an average cost of $2.93 per bushel. As a matter of fact, most of the farmers purchased the seed from their neighbours.

I understood that in certain sections the homestead inspectors looked after the distribution of the seed grain, which largely consisted of oats in that locality, in the district west of Edmonton. Very little wheat went into that country. I understood that the average price paid for oats was over 75 cents per bushel.

I think the hon. gentleman is probably correct in regard to the oats that were purchased. A very trifling quantity of wheat was distributed in that district. I do not know the price paid in that locality, but I was quoting the price paid on all these distributions.
Scientific Institutions-Department of thei Interior-Astronomical Surveys-To pay W. Simpson for special services performed at the. Dominion Astronomical Observatory from May 1 to October 31, 1916, inclusive, $500.

This is an item to pay to Mr. W. Simpson, who was the assistant to the late Dr. King. An item was voted every year of $1,000 for payment for these particular duties. After Dr. King's death the duties were performed by Mr. W. Simpson. It is not an additional sum, but the balance of Dr. King's vote.
Who is discharging the duties performed by the late Dr. King?

Dr. King had a triple position. He was chief astronomer, chief commissioner of the Geodetic Survey and chief commissioner of the International Boundary Survey. There are very few men qualified technically to occupy the triple position which he occupied. He was a man of superior accomplishments and attainments, and it is most difficult to fill his position. However, in our treaty with the United States there was a provision that, in the event of the death of this officer, the position should be filled forthwith, and Dr. King's position on the International Boundary Survey was filled by Mr. J. J. McArthur, who was second in command, or, really, in command, of the field of the Geodetic Survey. He was appointed to the Boundary Survey, and he is also acting head of the Geodetic Survey. No appointment has been made to the position of chief astronomer as yet.

Might we express the hope that, under all the circumstances, in the future the expenditures in the Astronomical Survey Department will show a less rate of increase than they have through the past year?
311i
Dominion Lands and Parks-Salaries of the Outside Service-further amount required, $20,000.

This is to increase the
salaries of the Dominion Lands Branch, in the outside service, similar to thait in the Immigration Service, and with a similar increase to the inside service; that is $100 increase per year to all those receiving a salary of $1,000.
Is that increase continued from year to year?
No, not from year to year, it was an increase for this year.
I suppose some of them get more than others?

Yes, some receive $65 a
month, some $50 and some $55.
But the increase would be proportionate to the salary they are receiving.

Yes. Of course increases do not apply to all of them.	.
Dominion Lands and Parks-Salaries of the commissioners to be appointed under the Soldiers' Settlement Act of 1917 to assist returned soldiers in settling- upon the land, $16,000.

This is to cover the salaries of the three commissioners to be appointed under the Soldiers' Settlement Bill which passed Parliament a few weeks ago, -in which it was provided that three commissioners should be appointed for the administration of that Act, the chairman of which was to draw $6,000 per annum, and the other two commissioners $5,000 each.
Have these two commissioners been appointed yet?

No, the Bill has not yet
received the Royal Assent.

Has the minister any
idea who they might be?

Not the slightest, but I
can assure my hon. friend they will be excellent men, because it is of great importance they should be.
Under no circumstances would 'they be partisans?
The Union Government would appoint them?
I will not say too much about it, because perhaps I may not have much to do about the appointment.

Six thousand dollars seems a large salary for a position of that

kind. You require a person who knows the work well, and who would know the best place to settle these men and give them practical assistance, but it does not follow that the kind of man who usually gets $6,000 salary is the man for that sort of job. A judge of the Supreme Court gets $6,000, but he would be a very poor agent to settle soldiers in the Northwest. He would not have the qualifications for that kind of work. There may be a man who will earn the money, but it seems to me it is-not the class of work that calls for such a high salary as $6,000 a year, which I suppose would carry travelling expenses, and other disbursements with it. I would like the minister to think over it, and see if, in view of present conditions, he could not get a man to do that work just as well as it could be done, with a smaller salary than $6,000 a year.

When the Soldiers' Settlement Bill was under discussion in the House, it was impressed upon me by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House how very essential it would be in order to make a success of this scheme, to have first-class men appointed. It was stated particularly by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney) that the success of this scheme largely will depend upon the personnel of the commission. It will be difficult to get a first-class man, without paying a good salary, because it is not a life job, like a judgeship, and it will take whoever we may appoint away from his ordinary avocation in life for the time he has to devote to it. My own idea is that the soldiers should have the nomination of one of these commissioners. They have asked for that privilege, and I think it is a reasonable request. The soldiers should be made jointly responsible for the administration of the Act.
I am satisfied that amongst returned soldiers could be found men who would fill a place on this commission to the satis' faction of the soldiers and of the country as a whole. It is essential that one of the men should be a trained and experienced agriculturist, and that the other should be a financial man who has had considerable experience in the lending business. As the position will not last a lifetime, it is desirable that the salaries of both commissioners shall be commensurate with the duties to bd performed.

If you engage an educationalist or a man high in some profession to take up work of this kind-to deal

with lands and new settlements in the West -it may be a new field of activity for him; he may have a good deal to learn. On the other hand, I would think that in the minister's department there would be men whose experience and training in connection with lands, settlement in the West and immigration would make their services exceedingly useful. I would suggest that he look over the list of men in his department whose experience and training qualify them for these positions.
Can the minister give the serial number of this particular commission in .the list of those which have been appointed since the Government took office?

This one is not yet appointed.
Advance to soldiers settling upon the land, and cost of administering the Soldiers' Settlement Act. 1917, including clerical assistance, $2,500,000.
Has the minister received any application for advances under the Soldiers' Settlement Act?

Yes, a number of applications have been received. We are awaiting the assent of His Excellency to the Bill and the appointment of the commission to administer the Act. We have put this amount in the Estimates with the idea that it will cover advances to those who locate on the land during the first year. We hope that we shall have to ask for more next session, because the larger the number of soldiers locating on the land the better for the country, as well as for the soldiers themselves.

Has the Government taken up the suggestion that I made on a previous occasion

that of expropriating unoccupied and unused lands contiguous to railways?

'Some consideration was given to that matter; some soldiers' deputations presented that aspect of the case to the Government by way of resolution of returned soldiers' associations. After discussing the matter with representatives of returned soldiers who waited upon myself and other members of the Government, we put this before them: in view of the fact that we do not know how many soldiers may desire to locate upon land, it would not be desirable for the Government at this time to expropriate a large acreage of land and incur the expenditure that would be involved in such a transaction. Under present conditions, if the soldier does not desire to go on free homestead land in the

western provinces, he has the opportunity of purchasing lands in any part of the country, and we will' assist him financially to purchase or equip the land. We suggested that that would be much better than our buying the land, because if we bought the land some soldiers might be satisfied and others dissatisfied. Some might not care to locate in a particular province or in a particular part of a province. We suggested that, at any Tate during the first ye'ar, any soldiers who had a little capital of their own and who desired to purchase land near transportation facilities and in a vicinity where population was comparatively dense might avail themselves of the privilege of selecting their own land and of receiving assistance from the Government by way of loan.
The limit of assistance to be that fixed by the Act?
That fixed by the Act.

In the case of the purchase of land, as I said on a previous occasion, the Government would be safe enough in making additional advances within the value of land that would give sufficient security. There would be no danger of loss to the Government if they .made some additional advances towards the purchase of the land so long as they kept within the margin of value.
It would be interesting to know the terms upon which the minister proposes to make these advances. What will be the rate of interest and how much will be advanced to any one person? '

That	is provided in the

Was the rate of interest
specified in the Bill?

Yes.

in the spring of 1903 a landslide from Turtle mountain took place entailing the lose of seventy lives of people in .the town of Frank, Alberta, together with the destruction of a large amount of property. According to recent observations, the danger of another landslide was found to be still more threatening, and it was decided to move the buildings from their present location to a safer site. A statement of the amounts of the contracts for moving the buildings has been prepared by Mr. Sterling who is looking after the interests of the provincial government, and the total cost will be $69,220, to be borne as follows:
By the Dominion Government .... $30,000 By the Provincial Government ....	20,000
By the owners	 19,220
This is the revote of the balance of the amount to be expended by the Dominion Government.
Is it intended to make a clearance of all the houses in danger, or is it just a matter left to the judgment of the owners of the houses?

The idea was to have all
the houses cleared away from the old site to a safe site.
Is this a compulsory clearance, or is it a clearance in the discretion of the occupants?

I do not think there was any compulsion further than persuasion, but I think generally-the owners have agreed to the movement. I do not know of any that have remained on the old site to run the risk of another land elide at some future date. We have had no necessity for using compulsion.	j

If houses are left in the
vicinity of a mine, it is quite likely that people will occupy them, and, of course, the lives of these people will be in danger.
We have done our utmost to have the houses moved, and we are not financially liable if houses are destroyed.
Why are we moving the houses at all? Can the minister be induced to do some house moving in any other part of Canada than Alberta? What is the explanation of our paying for the moving of houses?

Perhaps the hon. gentleman did not take cognizance of the statement of the case that I made. This was an arrangement made between the Provincial Government of Alberta and -the Dominion Government that they assume joint responsibility along with the owners for moving the houses away from a site which it was considered was dangerous for residence. Frank is a mining town, and it is absolutely necessary to have these houses moved away, because if they were allowed to remain there further loss of life might occur. The owners were not in a financial position to move their houses, and therefore, at the request o: the Provincial Government, the Dominion Government and the Provincial Government assumed joint responsibility, the Dominion Government, the Provincial Government and the owners bearing a lair proportion of the cost of removal.

In that part of the country from which I come, if a man starts a farm in a green forest, he has to make a clearing by cutting down the trees and he has to build a house. If he wants seed, he has to buy it. If he has not sufficient money, he has to go to the mines in order to earn enough money to buy seed. I find, however, that, in the West, not only does the Government build houses for the men, but if anything happens to a house, they will move it to another site, and if Providence happens to bring on a landslide, they will fix the landslide. If a man run-s short of seed, they will buy it for him and, I suppose, put it into his barn. I am afraid our people in the East will find this out, and there will then be no need for any agent, the people will flock to this land of Canaan presided over by the Minister of the Interior. Has the minister any particular right to take our money and apply it to the removing -of houses and the buying of seed without first asking our leave? That is a very nice thing to do, but the people

in my district will be looking for the same privilege.

Parliament has already sanctioned this.

Amount required as compensation to G. F. S. Townsend for the seoond-hand compressors sold at auction in 1914 by agency of department in Halifax, which were inadvertently broken in yard: before delivery to purchaser, $2,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The facts are these. In September, 1914, the department sold through its agent at Halifax to Mt. Frederick S. Townsend, of Halifax, for the sum of $748, which amount was paid to the

department, eleven second-hand compressors, which were reported by the chief engineer's branch of the department to be of no further use in the service. Mr. Townsend claims he succeeded immediately after the purchase, at considerable expense in travelling, etc., in selling one of the compressors for $500, and had the sale of three others well advanced at a profit of about $900. When Mr. Townsend came to obtain delivery of the compressors, he found that employees of the Department of the Naval Service, who required some scrap in an emergency, had dismantled a number of the compressors and made use of parts, not knowing that they had been disposed'of and were not the property of the department, and Mr. Townsend declined to accept delivery and requested to be reimbursed the amount of the purchase price, also loss of profit on sales, travelling expenses, interest on outlay and incidental expenses incurred. At that time both the Marine and Fisheries Department and the Naval Service were occupying the Naval Yard at Halifax. After the outbreak of war the yard was required for naval purposes entirely, and the Department of Marine and Fisheries was moved across to the other side of the harbour. The Naval Department, requiring some junk for certain purposes, took these compressors, not knowing that they had been sold to Mr. Townsend. After considerable .correspondence^, the department, on the 14th of July, 1916, offered Mr. Townsend, without prejudice, $1,500 in settlement of his claim, which offer he declined to accept, claiming that his loss was upward of $3,000, but on discussing the matter recently with the officers of the Department of the Naval Service and the Department of Marine and Fisheries he agreed to accept $2,500 in full settlement.
The purchasing agent considers that Mr. Townsend has a good and valid claim, but that in his opinion $2,000 would fully compensate him for all his loss, and he recommends the payment of this amount to Mr. Townsend. I have a report from the deputy minister concurring in that, and having looked into the matter myself, I think it is a fair and equitable settlement.
Who is Mr. Townsend?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is a junk dealer in Halifax. I do not know him personally, but I have met him once, and once only, and that was when I was in Halifax in December last with Mr. Bennett. Mr. Townsend called on me then about the matter.

How mudh did he pay
for the compressors?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: : He paid $748. We offered to settle for $1,500, but he refused that and asked for $2,500. After looking carefully into the matter, the purchasing agent thinks that $2,000 would toe a fair settlement. This meets with the approval of the deputy minister, and also has my concurrence.

Did he buy these machines as junk?
Mr. HAZElN: Yes.
He made a pretty good profit on them.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He made about $1,300. When the compressors were sold, tenders were asked for, and Mr. Townsend's was the highest.

It seems to me somebody has been very careless. In the first place, the goods were sold very much too cheap. If it turns out they are worth $2,000 they should not have been sold for $748. Having been sold, they should not have been taken by the Naval Department, but should have been set aside for the purchaser. Who was responsible for this blunder?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
: I admit there was carelessness about the matter. The goods were sold by Mr. Harvey, who is our agent at Halifax and has been for a good many years past. I am not saying he was to blame. He represented to us that $748 was the best figure that could be got, and it was on his recommendation and report that the goods were sold. The trouble occurred through the two departments using the yard at that time. The compressors were lying in the yards until Townsend should take them, and the naval people, who wanted them for the purposes I have mentioned, thought they were junk and used them. I do not think they should have taken them without the consent of the agent of the Marine and Fisheries Department. There is no doubt in my mind that this is a legitimate claim, and that being the case, there is nothing to do but settle on the best terms possible.
Compassionate allowance to Mrs. Josephine Hilyard, widow of the late Charles Hilyard, formerly keeper of Head Harbour light and fog alarm, N.B., who was drowned on the 3rd

February last when proceeding from the fog alarm to the dwelling connected with the light, while in the performance of his duties, $500.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The facts are these: On the 3rd of February last the late keeper left his house at 1 a.m. to go to the fog alarm station, and after having performed Ms duties left the station at 5 a.m., and was drowned on his way back home. There was a gully between his dwelling house and the lighthouse, which at high tide was full of water. Mr. Hilyard used to cross on a ledge of rock, and this time he fell in and was drowned. He was employed in the department for about ten years, and during that time proved a very efficient employee, doing some repairs, etc., to the station which under ordinary circumstances would have required the sending of men from St. John agency to carry on the work, and thus saved hundreds of dollars to the department. The late keeper left a widow and one child seven years old. The widow is in poor health and poor financial circumstances.
I think she should have been given more.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am disposed to agree with my hon. friend. As we are giving a compassionate allowance I think it ought not to be less than $1,000. I am not quite sure as to the procedure, but if I may, I beg to move that this amount be increased to , $1,000.

Another Estimate
should he brought down.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
