To pay expenses of suit, etc., in the case of McGillivray vs. Kimber, Sydney Pilotage authority, $2,821.05.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend from North Cape Breton ('Mr. McKenzie) is familiar with this item. I have discussed the matter with him. The facts are these: In April, 1912, the pilotage authority of Sydney dismissed one of its pilots, John A. McGillivray, for misconduct. In March, 1914, McGillivray brought action against the P'lotage authority for wrongful dismissal on the ground that the authority had not proceeded properly. On April 22 following, the action was tried at Sydney before Mr. Justice Drysdale who gave judgment in favour of the plaintiff for $1,800 damages. An appeal was taken from that judgment, as the action of the pilotage authority in dismissing the pilot was upheld by the Department of Justice, which accordingly appealed the case to the Supreme Court of
[Mr. Hazen.l
Nova Scotia. The Supreme .Court of Nova Scotia unanimously reversed IMr. Justice Drysdale's judgment, and dismissed the action. The plaintiff then appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada, and this appeal was allowed and the original judgment of Mr, Justice Drysdale was confirmed. The agent of the Department of Justice who had charge of the case, Mr. T. S. Rogers, K.C., of Halifax, urged an appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and permission for such an appeal was actually obtained on condition that the appellants pay all costs, including those of the respondent as between solicitor and client, whether the appeal was successful or not. As the amount of the judgment was only about $1,800, and the costs would have come to nearly four times that amount, it was hardly considered good business to go on with the appeal, so the appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council was not proceeded with owing to the very large expense it would entail and to the advice of the Deputy Minister of Justice that, while his own view of the case was unchanged, the success of an appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council was not free from doubt. The total amount of judgment and costs is $2,821.05, which I am asking Parliament to vote.

The amount to
'be voted includes the amount of the verdict?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It includes the amount of the verdict and the costs.
Are we responsible for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We considered, after con-"ultation with the Department of Justice, it was only fair and right that we should pay the amount.
I suppose the pilotage authority has no funds?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Has it any control over the pilot?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is like most of the pilot commissions, it can only pass by-laws and so on, and with the approval of the Governor in Council it puts those by-laws into effect. It conducts examinations of pilots, etc.
Has it any funds?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am not aware that it
has.

I am quite familiar
with this pilotage commission,
10 p.m. and they have no property or assets. The pilots are paid by dues which they get from the ships and which are divided up between them at the end of every month.
Ocean and River Service-Amount required to pay claims of Merryfield & Co., $242.23, and G. J. Frizzell, of Prince Rupert, B.C., $585.03, for provisions supplied to defaulting steward Alex. B. Gordon of the C.G.S. "Estevan," $S27.26.
What is the meaning of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend will perhaps remember that at several other sessions we have had small amounts like this. Contracts were entered into with the stewards on board the Government steamers to supply meals to the officers and to the men at so much per meal. The " Estevan " is a buoy steamer belonging to the department, in the service on the Pacific coast. The contract was entered into with the steward, who unfortunately did not pay his bills to the merchants with whom he dealt. The merchants always held that as he wore a government uniform, and was on a government boat, the Government was responsible for his bills. Some years ago the system prevailed by which the department paid for everything; the steward contracted the bills, and the department paid them. It was found that that was a very expensive method, and it was changed to the system of entering into a contract with the steward at so much per meal. This effected a very large saving. When the change was made we put up notices in the different ports where these steamers were likely to be, to the effect that the Government was not responsible for bills contracted by those stewards, but in some cases these notices escaped the attention of the merchants. In some instances we took bonds for the faithful performance by the stewards of their duty. We could not get any guarantee company to accept the responsibility, so we had to take personal bondsmen. Those bondsmen are reported on by the agents of the department in the different places, and as far as possible we endeavour to get bondsmen who are satisfactory. We have proceeded against some of these bondsmen and they paid up. Unfortunately, in this case, the bondsmen met with business reverses and were not able to pay the amount.

Why should not the
captain do the business?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The contract is made with the steward, who purchases the supplies. The captain has to look after the management and navigation of the ship.
I understand that, but, usually in the ship business the captain has control of the whole thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That has not been the
practice in the Marine Department for many years.
The old system has been abandoned.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It was abandoned because it was found to be a most extravagant practice1, which led to a great deal of waste. The officials of the department were all against it, and the result of the change has been very satisfactory, and has effected a very considerable economy.
What became of the defaulting steward?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He cleared off, to the United States, I think .
Was he not prosecuted?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We placed the matter in the hands, of the Department of Justice, asking that the necessary action be taken to recover the amount of these claims from the steward's sureties under the bond. These sureties were Annie Janet Gordon and Mary E. Lnxton, respectively wife and sister-in-law of Gordon. Action was brought and judgment registered against the real estate in Victoria belonging to the defendants, but it was discovered that there were mortgages outstanding against the real estate. Perhaps under normal conditions there might have been a surplus after satisfying the mortgages, but there was a depression in the value of real estate all over the country, as my hon. friend knows, and the amount of the mortgage was practically the value of the real estate.
Will the minister say how the steward gets, the money? Does the captain furnish the steward with money to purchase the supplies?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The steward, is the contractor. His contract is fifty cents a meal for men and .seventydive cents for the officers. He is paid by the department.
Is any precaution taken to guard against any recurrence of these troubles?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes. One precaution is to publish at the ports (where the vessel is likely to call an anouncement that the department will not he responsible for any debts contracted by the steward. We also try to secure a bond in the case of such steward. We tried to have a company do this but could not find one willing to undertake this class of business, so we have had to take individual bonds.

The minister will see
how easy .it would be for a steward to defraud merchants in a town. For instance, in my own town if a man in uniform from one of these ships entered a store he could have anything he wanted, as. the storekeeper would think that the. Government would be responsible. .

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We take all the precautions we can.
Arts and Agriculture, purchase of seed grain -Governor General's warrant, $500,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The first warrant was issued on October 7, 1916, before the opening of the session, for $400,009. The second for $800,000 was issued on December 14. It was then found that we were having large demands, not only from the West, hut also from Eastern Canada, and that we would likely require more money for oats, so on March 23, during the recess, this Governor General's warrant for $500,000 was issued. We have now advanced $1,400,000 to the commissioner at Regina, the head of the Se^d Purchasing Commission.:, and the total purchases amount to nearly that amount. We have turned into the Receiver General $1,401,299 up to August 21, and really have a surplus on hand. We shall make a considerable profit out of the transaction, although if the market had gone the other way we would have lost, as we sold at the purchasable, price plus the cost of bagging, cleaning and handling. We have a surplus of 50,000 bushels of oats and some wheat which we are selling at commercial rates.

Why were the Governor General's warrants issued at a time when Parliament was really in session? Parliament met in January, and in the following March $500,000 was drawn by Governor General's warrant. The minister must have known while Parliament was sitting that this money would be required.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No, it was only after the most thorough investigation by Mr. Oliark, the seed commissioner, that we found that the demand would be so strong that we would need the additional warrant.
Why did not the money drawn in September by Governor General's warrant appear in the main Estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: As a matter of fact, I find that it appeared in the Supplementary Estimates of the previous year, 1916-17.

The full explanaion given by the minister will be a sufficient warrant for the questions and the insistence of the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles). It was an important transaction, and it was very desirable that the House should be informed.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I thoroughly appreciate that.
Have all moneys advanced for 'the purchase of grain been returned?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes, and a little in addition. We shall make a profit on the transaction.

Compassionate allowance to the widow of the late Andrew Ryan, who was killed while in the performance of his duties as switchman on the Transcontinental Railway, December 22, 1916, $2,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Ryan was acting as a switchman on December 22 last. It appears that he fell off the car and a train backed over him. He leaves a wife and two children-a boy four years old and a girl nine months old-in very poor circumstances.
Progress reported.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Hazen, the House adjourned at 10.34 p.m.
Saturday, August 25, 1917.
